To award a contract for a period of 15 months
via Direct award to Vodafone for Lookout Advanced
 
Total Contract Costs =
£28,141.20
 
Funds covered by the forecasted budget

Lookout is our current mobile device security
software; the decision to renew it is to ensure our mobile device
estate ( mobile phones, tablets and chrome books)  remains
uptodate, resilient and protected against modern day cyber
risks.
 
The contract length is set to align with our
vodafone mobile voice and data service to allow us flexibility to
plan for future requirements in line with LGR plans.
 
Software
information:
 
Mobile Device Security: Lookout for
Work helps protect company data and devices from various security
threats. This includes safeguarding against malware, phishing
attacks, and other mobile-specific threats. By securing mobile
devices, businesses can reduce the risk of data breaches and
cyberattacks.
 
Data Protection: Adur and Worthing
councils deal with sensitive and confidential data. Lookout for
Work helps ensure that this data is protected, even when employees
access it on their mobile devices. 
 
Compliance: Requirements regarding the
protection of customer data. Mobile security solutions can help
businesses meet these compliance standards, avoiding costly fines
and legal issues.
 
Productivity: Lookout for Work can
enhance productivity by allowing employees to use their smartphones
for work-related tasks without the fear of compromising security.
This includes accessing email, documents, and other work-related
applications.
 
Lost or Stolen Device Recovery: In the
event that an employee's mobile device is lost or stolen, Lookout
for Work can help track and recover the device or remotely wipe
sensitive data to prevent unauthorised access.
 
Mobile Device Management (MDM): Using a
mobile device management solution with security apps like Lookout
for Work will allow us to manage and control mobile devices,
including configuring security settings, pushing updates, and
ensuring compliance with company policies.
 
Remote Work: With the rise of remote
work, employees are increasingly using their mobile devices to
access company resources. Mobile security solutions help extend
security to these remote endpoints, ensuring that employees can
work securely from anywhere.
 
Phishing Prevention: Phishing attacks
are a significant threat to businesses. Lookout for Work helps
protect employees from phishing scams by identifying and blocking
suspicious links and emails.
 
App and Network Security: Lookout for
Work can monitor the apps installed on devices and assess their
security risks. They can also protect against threats that may
arise from unsecured Wi-Fi networks or public hotspots.
 

Alternative providers would not be a
financially viable option particularly given the impending LGR.

Following the formal tender process, to award
the contract to Azone Projects Ltd (who
submitted the most advantageous tender) for up to £630,000
which includes a contingency to complete the aforementioned works
to improve the building, ready for reletting.

Eskan Court is
held by the Council under the Strategic Property Investment Fund.
Properties held through the SPIF are to support the Council
finances through income generation. This decision will enable the
space to be let, to assist in retaining the upper floor tenant upon
lease expiry, therefore retaining income.


1.   
Various approved contractors were initially considered for the
three formal tender invitations, and following consideration of the
project particulars and scope, Azone Projects, and two others
deemed most suitable to operate on this project type and scope
within the Milton Keynes area.
 
The scope of works tendered
can be summarised as the dilapidations and CAT A refurbishment
works to the Part Ground Floor unit, to include EPC upgrade works
to the base-build M&E/HVAC in anticipation of updated MEES
regulations. 
 

2.   
Leaving the site as it is. This option would mean the unit would
remain a vacant space without income to the Council and, crucially,
in future breach of MEES (Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards)
regulations so becoming unliveable.

To authorise the procurement of the works to
be executed by White Rock Construction Limited via a JCT Minor
Works Building Contract (2024 Edition) for necessary unit repairs
at T4, Dominion Way, Worthing with a maximum contract value of
£130,000, inclusive of all contingency funds.

T4 Dominion Way is held by the Council as a
Tier 2 asset to support the Council finances through income
generation. To enable the refurbishment of the unit to proceed so
that the unit may be re-let to generate income for the
Councils.

Leaving the site as it is. This would mean the
unit would remain vacant, meaning the Council would continue to pay
for void rates, as well as losing potential income from a new
tenant.

Before the Committee was a report by the
Service Director for Place and Economy, copies of which had been
circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to the
signed copy of these minutes as Item 8.
 
In late 2025, the Councils commissioned the
development of Economic Data for each local authority area,
together with the preparation of a refreshed Economic Strategy for
Adur and Worthing, and Arun. The previous strategy for the Councils
expired in 2023/24.
 
Following extensive data analysis, secondary
research, stakeholder interviews and consultation through SQW, the
draft Economic Strategy for Arun, Adur & Worthing 2026 - 2031
was put before Members for approval. The strategy was developed in
partnership with Arun District Council as the neighbouring coastal
West Sussex authority was on a similar timetable for their economic
strategy development, as well as having similarities in the coastal
economy.
 
The draft Strategy included Action Areas that
were focused on the five themes. These ensured that priorities were
addressed in a coherent and mutually-reinforcing way, help build
resilience, create distinctiveness and deliver significant economic
impact: ? Advancing advanced manufacturing ? Growing the leisure,
hospitality and cultural economy ? Building the green economy ?
Encouraging enterprise ? Promoting and nurturing our places
 
Members discussed the strategy and felt that
more emphasis needed to be placed upon the contribution made by
farming to the local economy including food security, nature
recovery and economic growth. The Service Director for Place and
Economy acknowledged that he could make relevant changes to the
document.
 
Decision:
 

1.   
That the Arun, Adur and Worthing Economic Draft Strategy 2026 -
2031 be approved  and the five economic
themes and distinct Action Areas be approved, that it
be  delegated to the Service Director
for Place & Economy, in consultation with the Leaders and
Cabinet Members for Regeneration, to complete the final document,
including any final amendments .
 

2.   
That the economic data that supports the draft Strategy be noted
with a number of these evidence bases being available through West
Sussex County Council to assist with monitoring data and trends
over the lifetime of the plan.
 

3.   
That it be noted that the draft Strategy and economic data have
been developed in partnership with Arun District Council with Local
Government Reorganisation (LGR) and Devolution in mind.

Before the Committee was a report by the
Service Director for Place and Economy, copies of which had been
circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to the
signed copy of these minutes as Item 11.
 
The report before Members sought agreement to
proposed constitutional and delegation changes required to support
effective local plan-making under the new statutory 30-month
plan-making system.
 
The output of the decision would be a clearer
governance framework for plan preparation at Adur & Worthing
Councils, including: clarification of the status of statutory
planning documents within the Councils’ Policy Framework,
amendments to the Scheme of Sub-Delegations to include explicit
planning policy functions c. adopting the comprehensive
decision-making framework for the main stages of plan preparation
set out in Appendix 1, delegated authority for technical,
procedural, and data-driven plan-making documents where
appropriate.
 
The plan-making system contained closely
sequenced statutory stages and Gateway requirements. Clear decision
routes were required at the outset to reduce the risk of delay,
uncertainty, or avoidable re-reporting during plan preparation.
 
Members were asked to consider the
implications of the new plan-making system for Adur and Worthing,
given the context of Local Government Review.
 
 
Decision:
 

1.   
That the formal introduction of the reformed local plan-making
system and the statutory requirement for local planning authorities
to design governance frameworks capable of ensuring a plan can be
found sound and adopted within a 30-month timeframe be noted.
 

2.   
That it be recommended to each Council the approval of the
comprehensive plan-making governance and sign-off pathway set out
in Appendix 1, and targeted amendments to the Scheme of
Sub-Delegations to introduce explicit planning policy delegations
for the Head of Planning and the Planning Policy and Specialists
Manager to give effect to that pathway.
 

3.   
That it be recommended to each Council that planning policy
consultation responses (including responses to Neighbourhood Plans
and strategic external planning consultations) be formally
separated from development management consultation chains within
the Scheme of Sub-Delegations, with authority delegated to
appropriate planning policy officers in consultation with the
relevant Cabinet Member(s) where strategic issues arise.
 

4.   
That Subject to Local government reorganisation, Council Leaders
formally contact the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local
Government (MHCLG) and seek to discuss a pragmatic approach to
plan-making given the potential of joint local plan with other
authorities, in the context of Local Government Reorganisation
timings in Sussex.
 

5.   
That the Councils agree to continue discussions regarding
plan-making with other local authorities within the proposed
Unitary area if or when the geography is confirmed.
 
 

6.   
That it be recommended to each Council that the Monitoring Officer
be authorised to amend the constitutions in consultation with the
Head of Planning to incorporate necessary amendments arising from
the reformed local plan making system and changes arising from the
legislation. Such amendments will also include any necessary
updates to the Scheme of Delegations. As is usual procedure, the
updates will be reported through the Joint Audit and Governance
Committee through to Full Councils for review.

Council are not subject to call-in

Before the Committee was a report by the
Corporate Director for Housing and Communities, copies of which had
been circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to
the signed copy of these minutes as Item 12.
 
The report before Members set out the options
for a Members' decision on the Adur and
Worthing Wellbeing Programme, which has been in place since 2011,
delivering healthy lifestyle interventions for communities,
particularly focusing on health inequalities.
 
The programme formed an important part of the
Councils’ health and wellbeing programmes and is externally
funded by Public Health and delivered through respective
partnership agreements between each of the District and Borough
Councils and West Sussex County Council (WSCC). The current
agreements are due to expire 31 March 2027. WSCC agreed in March of
this year to a variation of the current partnership agreements and
extension for an additional two years to 31 March 2029.
 
Members were updated on the progress made and
provided a recommended option to extend the Partnership Agreements
for both Adur and Worthing programmes for an additional two years,
subject to funding being agreed on an annual basis, to March 2029.
It proposed that the development and approval of the annual
business plan accompanying those agreements be delegated to the
Corporate Director for Housing and Communities in consultation with
the Cabinet Members for Community Wellbeing and Leisure.
 
Decision:
 

1.   
That the progress made by the Wellbeing Programme in Adur and
Worthing be noted;
 

2.   
That the preferred option to extend the two Partnership Agreements
be approved for the Adur and Worthing Wellbeing Programme for a
further two years from 1 April 2027 to 31 March 2029 between Adur
District Council and WSCC and between Worthing Borough Council and
WSCC, to deliver the Wellbeing programme subject to funding being
agreed on an annual basis;
 

3.   
That authority be delegated to enter into the Adur Partnership
Agreement and the Worthing Partnership Agreement with West Sussex
County Council, to the Director for Housing and Communities, in
consultation with the Cabinet Members for Community Wellbeing and
Leisure;
 

4.   
That authority be delegated to to agree
the draft annual business plan to the Director for Housing and
Communities in consultation with the Cabinet Members for Community
Wellbeing and Leisure;
 

5.   
That it be agreed to receive the annual funding allocation from
West Sussex County Council for the next two years of the
partnership agreement and to recommend to the Councils to amend the
revenue budget accordingly. The indicative annual amount from WSCC
for 2027-2029 is £566,769 for Adur and Worthing with further
detail given in section 6 of the attached report.
 

6.   
That an in-kind contribution provided by the Councils’ be agreed, as detailed at 6.5 in the
report, to continue.

Before the Committee was a report by the Chief
Executive, copies of which had been circulated to all Members and a
copy of which is attached to the signed copy of these minutes as
Item 9.
 
The Fair, Green & Local Plan had guided
the work of the councils effectively over the previous year, with
project delivery a key focus. Successes were outlined in the report
to the Committee, It was important to note that improved governance
and project management had strengthened the councils’ ability
to deliver.
 
Over the preceding year, both councils had
been engaged in the local government reorganisation process,
working with other West Sussex local authorities. The practical
programme of transition work to the new unitary councils was
expected to intensify following the decision by the Secretary of
State regarding unitary boundaries expected in October 2026. The
Fair, Green & Local LGR mission was in place to help coordinate
the councils’ work in this area.
 
The councils had taken a proactive approach to
the opportunities of LGR. A cross-party working group was convened
over a number of months to consider the future of neighbourhood
governance, reporting to Full Councils in March 2026. Broader
engagement was also undertaken with community leaders through the
‘Thriving Together’ mission, bringing out a set of
“People’s Priorities”, and creating a valuable
platform for future developments.
 
These people’s priorities had shaped
Fair, Green & Local, and the report set out the intention of
both councils to focus further on the issues that matter most to
our communities - moving ‘from talk to action’. The
report recommended that the Thriving Together mission had evolved
into ‘Pride in Place’, marrying participation with
practical community action. The revised mission provided for a
continuation of community participation work through the
development of new inclusive engagement plans, while re-allocating
neighbourhood team projects from other missions under Pride in
Place.
 
 
 
Decision:
 

1.   
That the revision of the Thriving Together mission to Pride in
Place be approved
 

2.   
That the proposed actions and re-allocations of projects to the
revised mission block be approved.
 

3.   
That the rapid development of the West Sussex Local Government
Reorganisation (LGR) programme currently underway be noted, which
is expected to require an increased level of local resourcing. This
is expected to require a rebalancing of effort in the coming 18
months, and this will be set out in more detail at the next update
in December 2026.
 

4.   
That the significant progress with actions across the FGL delivery
plan be noted, along with the additional steps taken to further
strengthen programme governance and risk management.
 

5.   
That the Corporate Plan be referred to Adur District and Worthing
Borough Councils for Members to note and endorse the updates,
including the evolution of Thriving Together into Pride and Place
and the re-allocation of related actions to this newly named
mission area.

Before the Committee was a report by the
Corporate Director for Housing and Communities, copies of which had
been circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to
the signed copy of these minutes as Item 13.
 
The Housing Strategy 2025–2030 had
guided the work of both councils over the preceding 18 months,
reflecting a fundamental commitment to fairness by treating good
quality housing as a basic human right essential for dignity,
health, and thriving communities. Providing a decent and affordable
home for everyone living in Adur and Worthing was an important
task, but also our biggest challenge. The reasons for Adur and
Worthing's housing shortage are complex, affected by both national
and local issues. This housing crisis impacts nearly every part of
residents' lives.
 
The Housing Strategy set out six strategic
priorities to improve housing, providing focus and drive through a
five-year framework to improve housing quality, support health and
wellbeing, and guide future local development. It was developed
against a backdrop of continued and immense demand for new and
existing housing, a critical lack of move-on options especially for
Worthing and severe financial pressures tied to temporary
accommodation. A primary focus remained on increasing the supply of
genuinely affordable homes and improving council housing quality
for social homes in Adur. Alongside this were a
number of sweeping new national policy changes, including on
Renters Rights and Supported Housing reforms.
 
The Housing Strategy recognised the shared
opportunities and challenges across Adur and Worthing and the
distinct nature of both places and their differences. Adur being a
stock-holding council offered both opportunities and challenges
with the statutory responsibilities and stock condition needs of a
social landlord. Worthing managed extreme land constraints, higher
homelessness presentations, and a more acute budget strain.
Delivering against these separate local needs required tailored
operational approaches, strong multi-agency partnerships, and
proactive, data-led interventions.
 
Local Government Reorganisation (LGR)
framework remained a key pillar for future direction, creating a
distinct opportunity to remodel how housing services are designed
with Social Care and other services across a wider footprint.
 
Decision:
 

1.   
That the progress made on the first 18 months of the Housing
Strategy Delivery Plan be noted;
 

2.   
That it be noted that a Housing Strategy progress report will be
provided on an annual basis, with the next one being summer
2027;
 

3.   
That it be noted that there is an ongoing delegation to the
Corporate Director for Communities and Housing, in consultation
with each Councils’ Cabinet Members for Housing to make minor
amendments to the Strategy delivery plan, as required, for example,
in response to significant changes in service demands or national
legislative changes.
 
 
Call In: The call-in deadline for
decisions will be 5.00pm on 18 September 2026.

Before the Committee was a report by the Chief
Governance Officer, copies of which had been circulated to all
Members and a copy of which is attached to the signed copy of these
minutes as Item 15.
 
The report before Members informed the Joint
Strategic Committee of a Motion which was supported by Worthing
Borough Council following a vote at its meeting on 16th December
2025. The Motion titled, Artificial Intelligence in Local
Government Ethics, was reproduced (as amended) at Appendix 1.
 
Members generally supported the principals
behind the motion, however, it was felt
that there was no current need to create a significant new strategy
or programme of works. Much of the work was underway. Capacity and
resource was a consideration whenever
approving new work streams particularly when there was uncertainty
in light of local government
reorganisation
 
It was agreed that the relevant ethical
principles continue to be considered though the AI user policy that
was being developed and that the wider approach to AI governance be
kept under review as technology and the use of it developed. This
would include appropriate engagement with staff, unions, residents
and elected members where relevant
 
 
Decision:
 

1.   
That the ethical principles within the motion be noted and that it
be agreed that the relevant ethical principles continue to be
considered though the AI user policy that is being developed, and
that the wider approach to AI governance be kept under review as
technology and the use of it develops. This will include
appropriate engagement with staff, unions, residents and elected
members where relevant

decisions will be 5.00pm on 18 September 2026.

The report before Members set out a motion
(attached as Appendix 1) referred from the meeting of Worthing

Members noted that West Sussex County Council
had launched a consultation on delivering Climate action plan
subsequent to the motion. It was opined that the motion was more
appropriate for a County wide response that would allow the greater
region to apply for large scale national funds.
 
It was agreed that the motion would be
referred to the West Sussex Climate change board for the
board’s consideration and that the Cabinet would submit a
response to the West Sussex climate change mitigation and
adaptation consultation including the contents of the motion.
 
 
Decision:
 

1.   
That the motion be rejected reluctantly;
 

2.   
That the motion be referred to the West Sussex Climate Change
Board
 

3.   
That the Cabinet submit a response to the West Sussex climate
change mitigation and adaptation consultation including the
contents of the motion.
 
 
Call In: The call-in deadline for
decisions will be 5.00pm on 18 September 2026.

Other systems have been explored, demonstrated

The Assistant Director, finance will enter
into the contract with Access Paysuite Limited to deliver income
management and payment gateway services to the council for a period
of up to 3 years.

The council currently collects and allocates
all of its income through the pay 360 suite, a software as a
service (SaaS) solution provided by Access Paysuite Ltd. The
contract for this service was let on the 1st of September 2023 and
ran for a period of three years to the 31st of August 2026. This
contract is due to expire and in order to continue maintaining the
council's key income streams this system's contract needs to be
renewed.
 
The contract renewal will renew the existing
software licenses for three years (the minimum term allowed by the
supplier) ensuring that the council can accept payments up to and
including a transition period into local government
reorganisation. 
 
Over the last year finance officers have been
working with the incumbent supplier to address some issues with
business payment cards. Within the proposed new contract is the
renewal of the existing software. Some improvements were considered
but have not yet been tested with enough detail to implement such
as charging for commercial card use and open banking. 
 
Under the council's contract standing order a
contract of this value would require officers to seek 5 quotes or
use a compliant framework / Dynamic Marketplace. This appointment
is to be made via procurement for housing (pfh) framework for
payment software. This Framework allows for direct award to
suppliers and is compliant with both the councils contract standing
orders and The Procurement Act 2023. All fees collected by pfh
frameworks are used to support the creation of further compliant
routes to market for the public sector.
 

Change provider via a competitive process:
This process would take roughly 12 months and based on the market
for this service there is not a significant difference in value
between suppliers. We would however expect the process of setting
up a new supplier to be resource intensive for finance, digital,
legal and procurement officers. Without a significant reason to do
so we do not feel that this is the right approach particularly in
light of the upcoming changes required in this space for local
government reorganisation.
 
Do nothing: Payments received by the council
would need to be processed and allocated manually, currently the
finance team does not have the internal resources to do this. The
required recruitment to fill this role would significantly offset
the savings made by not purchasing the renewed contract.

Adur and Worthing enter into a service
agreement with Forvis Mazars LLP for provision of internal audit
services through a call of from the framework access agreement with
Croydon Borough Council.  The cost of the service is circa
£100,000 per annum.  The council provision for internal
audit services will be required until 31.3.2028.
 

The council to contract for Internal Audit
provision is a financial governance requirement. 
 
Croydon, as a local authority, is a body which
can publicly procure works, goods and services for itself and for
the benefit of other public bodies.  A previous framework
agreement expired 31.3.26 and the council needs to agree a contract
for ongoing internal audit provision. Currently is has agreed a
rolling agreement directly with Forvis Mazars LLP.
 
Following an advertisement on Croydon’s
eprocurement portal Intend and the Governments Central Digital
Platform and carrying out a tender process, Croydon has entered
into a new Framework Agreement with the Forvis Mazars LLP
(Contractor) for the provision of internal audit and anti-fraud
services from 1.4.26 to 31.03.2030.
 
Adur and Worthing council is to receive the
benefit of the Services directly from the Forvis Mazars and to use
the (Apex) Framework Agreement to allow the Services to be provided
by the contractor directly to Adur and Worthing Councils under a
Service Order.
 
Croydon will manage the overall provision of
the Services by the contractor in accordance with the Framework
Agreement; and Adur and Worthing Council will manage the provision
of the Services which are set out in the relevant Service Order
directly with the Contractor and shall also pay the Contractor
directly for the Services covered by the relevant Service
Order.
 
The service agreement for internal audit will
be required until 31.3.2028 when the councils will transition to a
new unitary authority through the Local Government Reorganisation
programme.
 

The council is required to have independent
financial governance and process reviews in place through an
internal audit service. The alternative would be to either recruit
internal resource but this would limit the scale of expertise that
could be utilised compared to the provision from a larger provider.
The council could do a full procurement exercise however it may
disrupt the delivery of audit service if there was transition to a
new provider.  And the effort is disproportionate when the
framework contract has been through a procurement exercise. The
service is provided through call off from the framework and is
renewed on an annual basis.

involvement in the project we recommend direct appointment to
ensure delivery within the required timescales.

feasibility has a marginal declared interest in the operation of

process was undertaken to ensure best value. The Council sought
three quotes inclusive of the previously involved quantity
surveyor, the average price was £26,133.00 with the winner

Cove Consulting at £26,500.00
 


Appointment of a single

London or Manchester based and for a project of this size would
generally have higher overheads and would not be able to provide as
hands on support as local consultants. 
Discharge the duties directly to
Ropetackle CIC for delivery; this was considered but the council is
liable for the funding requirements and would therefore need to
retain contractual control of the delivery.

To appoint Clarke Roofing Southern Ltd to
undertake Phase 1 of repairs to the Town Hall roof coverings for
the sum of £79,916.00 (exc
VAT).

The Town Hall Roof is currently being affected
by water ingress to two areas, firstly the rolled lead sheet
covering to the portico roof above the four pillars to the front
facade, where it intersects with the main part of the roof, is
leaking to the extent where the timber valley rafter beneath has
decayed quite substantially meaning some timber structural repairs
are required including the replacement of the timber valley rafter
itself subject Listed Building Consent/Conservation Officer
Approval. In addition to this, to the Southwest corner of the
building where the slate roof butts onto the Council chamber, there
is water ingress believed to be taking place in
the area of the existing cover flashings as well as the
fixed roof light that is in close
proximity. 
 
So as to prevent
further damage it is proposed to replace the rolled lead sheet
covering to the portico roof, strip back the Westmorland Slates at
the roof intersection and replace/undertake structural repairs to
the timber roof structure that has decayed. 
 
To the Southwest corner of the building it is proposed to remove the lead cover
flashings and soakers, by stripping back the Westmorland Slates,
re-build this area using new lead soakers and cover flashings and
redress the slates. At the same time an intrusive inspection of the
fixed roof light will be undertaken so as
to determine and address any water ingress to this area
until such the main part of the roof is worked upon in the months
ahead.
 
This work is required to prevent further water
damage taking place to Town Hall which is a Grade II Listed
Structure.
 

There are no alternative options

To award the joint contract for the Housing
Benefit Assurance Process (HBAP) audit service to KPMG LLP for an
estimated total contract value of £70,140 (Ex VAT). The
contract will commence on 20th September 2026 for an initial term

The Councils have a statutory obligation

certify the Council's annual Housing Benefit subsidy claim.

advantageous tender, offering the best value for money for the

withholding or loss of vital Housing Benefit Subsidy Funding. This
would create an unsustainable financial pressure at the
Councils. 
In House Provision: Rejected as the
HBAP audit must be conducted by an independent, appropriately
qualified, and registered external audit firm in accordance with
DWP specifications.

decision_maker: Service Director for Operations & Environmental Services (CLT)
content:
To award a contract to Envirotec for 2 years
with the option of 2 further years via direct award under the EEM
framework

The council surveyors team currently provides
support to the councils owned, commercial and housing properties
with regards to management of asbestos. This service required
specialist surveying, air testing and record keeping which is
currently outsourced to a specialist contractor Environtec
Limited. 
 
The Council's current contract with Environtec
expires in July 2026 and in order to continue with service delivery
a new contract is required. The management of asbestos is a
statutory duty as is the keeping of appropriate records, this is
essential to ensuring that we can provide contractors working on
our properties with up to date, compliant and factual records in
accordance with CAR2012 (Control of asbestos regulations
2012). 
 
Environtec are currently integrated with the
councils asbestos record keeping software system teams which the
surveyors team has been working to create with Environtec since
2021/2022. It is considered to be working to a high standard with
no ongoing issues. The council would therefore seek to continue its
current relationship with Environtec. Given the anticipated spend
of £160k over 4 years under the councils contract standing
orders we should either; undertake a competitive procurement
exercise seeking no less than 5 quotes or use an existing complaint
framework agreement (direct award or mini-competition).
 
Environtec are available for direct award
under several frameworks with competitively tendered fixed prices,
the most suitable framework (due to its contractual flexibility and
low % fee) is the Efficiency East Midlands framework EEM0024
Asbestos Surveys & Removals Framework.
 


Do nothing - This would lead to a
failure in our statutory duty to maintain asbestos compliance and
potentially put our staff and contractors in harm's way. 
Run a competitive procurement
procedure - This approach would potentially give us better rates
however we would need to train and integrate any new provider on
the team's software which can take up to 6 months.
topline: The Service Director for Operations & Environmental Services has decided to award a contract to Envirotec for asbestos management services.

content:
To complete the transfer of part of the
Council’s Freehold land HM Land Registry Title WSX298213 at
Land on the West Side of Long Furlong, Clapham, Worthing. The land
is not within the administrative area of Worthing Borough
Council.
 
The parcel to be sold comprises 24.39 acres of
arable land. The Council will retain the remaining 29.84 acres of
rough pastureland. There are no rights of way that affect the land
to be sold. The proposed purchaser is the current tenant, who has
occupied both parts of the land under one Agricultural Holdings Act
(AHA) tenancy for several decades and has security of tenure
rights. 
 
It has been agreed that, as part of this land
sale, the tenant will surrender their AHA agreement of the retained
rough pastureland for the Council to use for its own purposes (yet
to be decided). A sale price of £140,000 (One Hundred and
Forty Thousand Pounds) has been agreed, with the sale to complete
as soon as possible. 
 
In accordance with Section 123 of the Local
Government Act 1972, council officers have ensured ‘best
consideration’ is achieved for the disposal by obtaining an
independent RICS ‘Red Book’ Valuation by an
agricultural specialist. This valuation was updated in May
‘26 to confirm best consideration is still achieved.
 

In accordance with the Council’s
published ‘Disposals Strategy and Process’, this parcel
of land was identified as suitable for disposal as it is low income
producing, has no community or social value that warrants the
Council owning it, and there is no reasonable prospect of the land
being developed for emergency or temporary accommodation or social
housing (as the land is subject to the South Downs National Park
Planning Authority and is within an area of open countryside).
 
The Council’s legal officers have
confirmed there are no restrictions that create a legal impediment
to the sale. Furthermore, there were no other bona fide internal
uses identified, no community or environmental benefit to retaining
the land, and no strategic or council objective that would impede
the sale. 


1.   
Freehold sale of land of the entire land parcel with vacant
possession: This would require the surrender of the current
tenancy, which has significant statutory protection.
 

2.   
Freehold sale of land of the entire land parcel subject to the
existing Agricultural Holdings Act tenancy: This has been
discounted as WBC wishes to retain the rough pastureland for a
future use.
 

3.   
Freehold sale of the arable land only to the existing tenant and
WBC retaining the pastureland, which itself would still be subject
to the AHA tenancy which would have to be renegotiated. This would
result in less capital receipt for WBC than the recommended
proposal and less overall retained value of the pastureland.
topline: The Service Director for Place & Economy has decided to sell part of the Council's freehold land to the current tenant, retaining the remaining rough pastureland.

content:
To complete the Freehold sale of agricultural
land at Charmandean Quarry,
Off Charmandean Lane, Worthing, BN14
9NN, HM Land Registry Title WSX292097. 
 
Formerly a disused chalk pit, the land
comprises a total area of 0.77 hectares or 1.91 acres and includes
a farmyard, barn and stable buildings. The purchaser is the current
tenant, who has occupied on a Farm Business Tenancy for a period of
10 years from 5 October 2018. The proposal is to sell the land to
the tenant for  £330,000
(Three Hundred and Thirty Thousand Pounds), subject to the existing
lease. There are no rights of way across the land to be
sold. 
 
Per Section 123 of the Local Government Act
1972, council officers have ensured best consideration is achieved
for the transfer by obtaining an independent third-party valuation
by an agricultural specialist who has complied with RICS ‘Red
Book’ Valuation standards. This valuation was refreshed to
confirm best consideration is still achieved. 
 
It is proposed the transfer is completed at
the earliest opportunity.
 

In accordance with the Council’s
published ‘Disposals Strategy and Process’, this parcel
of land was identified as suitable for disposal as it is low income
producing, has no community or social value that warrants the
Council owning it, and there is no reasonable prospect of the land
being developed for emergency or temporary accommodation or social
housing (due to its origin as a quarry and unsuitable
access). 
 
The Council’s legal officers have
confirmed there are no restrictions that create a legal impediment
to the sale. Furthermore, there were no other bona fide internal
uses identified, no community or environmental benefit to retaining
the land, and no strategic or council objective that would impede
the sale.
 

As follows: 

1.   
Continue to let the land. This does not comply with the
Council’s Disposal Strategy as the site offers no
long term value to the organisation or
provide an exceptional upside to help support council services
other than a modest income eclipsed by the potential for a freehold
transfer.
 

2.   
Sell the land with vacant possession. The Council would need to
wait until 2028 for the expiry of the Farm Business Tenancy.
“A bird in the hand principle” applies: The anticipated
sale price with vacant possession may or may not decline over the
next 2 years. Capital now is worth more to the Council than the
prospect of obtaining a speculative amount in the future. 
 

3.   
Market the land more widely and sell the land to another purchaser,
subject to the existing Farm Business Tenancy.  This would
generate less return and create uncertainty for our
tenant.
topline: The Service Director for Place & Economy has decided to complete the Freehold sale of agricultural land at Charmandean Quarry in Worthing, UK.

Under the executed sale agreement between WBC
and Roffey Homes, the Council may be called upon to facilitate the

To grant easements and restrictive covenant
rights (“the Rights over land within HM Land Registry Title

transferred to MUA Electricity Limited (“MUA
Electricity”) by Roffey Homes Limited (“Roffey

The Council owns the freehold to
the Access Land which serves the Union Gardens development. The
Council has been requested by Roffey Homes (in accordance with the
terms of the sale contract between the Council and Roffey Homes re
the Union Gardens development land) to enter into the transfer deed
as ‘Grantor’ (acting in its capacity as freeholder of

Eastern Power Networks. The Rights granted are:
 


easements [set
out at clause 12.2 of the transfer] which include a right of way over part of the
Access Land and the right to lay electricity cables under the same;
and

restrictive covenants over part of
the Access Land relating to alterations for the protection of the
electric lines to be installed [set out at
clause 12.5 of the transfer].

 

As the Director for Service has assessed the
proposed transfer terms as being within the type of agreement that
the developer may require under the sale contract, not progressing

Before the Committee was a report by the
Service Director for Place and Economy, copies of which had been
circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to the
signed copy of these minutes as Item 11.
 
The report before Members proposed a new,
pooled approach to community funding across Adur and Worthing from
2026/27. The proposal aimed to consolidate fragmented funding
streams into a single, cohesive programme with a "single front
door" for applicants, shared principles, and consistent assessment
processes, while maintaining area-based funding distinctions.
 
The current grants landscape involved multiple
funding pots with varying histories, criteria, and administrative
processes across Council teams. Engagement with community groups
and recent evaluations (e.g., Worthing CIL Neighbourhood Fund,
Kitchen Table, Thriving Together) indicated that the model created
administrative complexity and hindered impact.
 
The proposed pooled model sought to simplify
access by creating a clearer route for applicants, reducing
duplication and confusion. It aimed to increase impact, by shifting
focus toward long-term community benefit, capacity building, and
project legacy rather than isolated, short-term activities.
Streamlining officer time and resource allocation by unifying
administrative frameworks will improve efficiency. Finally, it
would ensure consistent, transparent decision-making that aligns
with the Council’s Fair, Green & Local strategic
priorities.
 
The programme would be delivered in two
phases. Phase 1 (2026/27) introduced a single application route,
shared assessment criteria, and local assessment panels (bringing
together ward councillors, officers, and community representatives)
for each area. This phase included a pilot of the Plinth grants
management platform to test digital streamlining and monitoring.
Phase 2 utilised learning from the first round to co-design further
improvements with the Voluntary, Community, and Social Enterprise
(VCSE) sector. This would explore enhanced digital tools, simpler
monitoring, and tailored support for emerging groups.
 
Decision:
 

1.    
That the creation of the Adur & Worthing Community Grants
Programme as a pooled community funding approach for 2026/27 and
beyond be approved, bringing together the in-scope funding streams
set out in this report.
 

2.    
That the proposed objectives and principles for the programme be
approved, including lasting community benefit, collaboration,
accessibility, local impact, fairness, and alignment with Fair,
Green & Local priorities.
 

3.    
That the proposed Phase 1 process and timetable for the 2026/27
funding round be approved, including local networking events, a
single application route, local assessment panels and Cabinet
Member reports for final award decisions.
 

4.    
That the proposed funding allocations by area for Adur and
Worthing, as set out in the table in section 6 of this report be
approved.
 

5.    
That virements be approved of up to the following amounts from the
Worthing CIL Neighbourhood Fund per Worthing CIL Area, for awarding
funding to groups following the CIL Assessment Panels and sign-off
via Cabinet Member report:
 
a.    
Coastal East: £39,873.27
 
b.    
Coastal West: £20,730.94
 
c.    
North: £12,845.89
 

6.    
That authority be delegated to the relevant Cabinet Members to
approve final grant awards following the recommendation from the
assessment panels.
 

7.    
That it be noted that officers will bring forward a Phase 2 update
after the first pooled funding round, including learning from the
process, the Plinth pilot, feedback from voluntary community &
social enterprise (VCSE) organisations, and options for further
simplifying and strengthening the programme.
 
 
Call In: The call-in deadline for
decisions will be 5.00pm on 23 July 2026.
topline: The Joint Strategic Committee has decided to approve the creation of the Adur & Worthing Community Grants Programme for 2026/27 and beyond, aiming to consolidate funding streams and improve efficiency.

Before the Committee was a report by the
Corporate Director for Housing and Communities, copies of which had
been circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to
the signed copy of these minutes as Item 12.
 
The Albion Street development would provide 49
energy-efficient, desirable homes. It formed part of what has been,
up until this point, a largely successful development programme for
Adur Homes, which had resulted in the provision of 26 homes in
Sompting, Lancing, Shoreham and
Fishersgate for local residents since 2024. A
number of issues and challenges had come to light with the
development, following the insolvency of the contractor. Due to
issues with water penetration in several locations within the last
several months, extensive intrusive investigations were
commissioned to confirm the building's integrity, which have
revealed significant and complex construction defects that needed
to be resolved before the homes could be safely occupied.
 
The report before Members set out those
issues, which included design features that inadvertently funnelled
rainwater into the structure, alongside faulty damp course
installations and the use of materials not fully suited to the
highly exposed coastal environment. Taken together, those issues
required significant remedial work. They needed to be addressed
systematically rather than applying superficial repairs to ensure
that they fully addressed those issues before the building was
occupied.
 
The overall increased costs for the Albion
Street project were estimated to total £3.2 million. The
estimated figure was subject to ongoing overview by the project's
cost consultants and included £2.1m to address extensive
remedial works, £400,000 for professional costs and
£700,000 allowance for capitalised interest associated with
the borrowing required for the project.
 
The report also set out the approach with
tenants who were currently waiting to occupy the development to
keep them informed and support them throughout the process. A
further report with lessons-learned would be brought back to
Members.
 
Decision:
 

1.    
That the following virements be approved in the 2026/27 capital
programme of:
 
a.    
£2 million to Albion Street capital project budget.
(£1.3 million for construction works and professional Fees
and £700,000 capitalised interest). Funded by:
 
b.    
£450,000 from Electrical Works budget,
 
c.    
£400,000 from the Reactive Works budget,
 
d.    
£900,000 from the Kitchens and Bathrooms budget, and
 
e.    
£250,000 from the Structural Work budget.
 

2.    
That a budget for £1.2m be approved for the remaining
estimated cost to complete the remedial works for the Albion Street
scheme from the overall 2027/28 capital budget allowance as a
priority project within the programme.
 

3.    
That it be noted that this will enable officers to proceed with the
procurement and execution of essential remedial works as a matter
of urgency as we continue to progress the building toward a
habitable condition.
 

4.    
That authority be delegated to the Corporate Director for Housing
and Communities to procure and enter
into or extend all necessary contracts and associated legal
documentation and to seek and to accept any relevant grant funding
in order to deliver these works and
enable the project to progress within the approved budget.

decisions will be 5.00pm on 23 July 2026.
topline: The Joint Strategic Committee has decided to approve additional funding for remedial works on the Albion Street development to address significant construction defects and ensure the safety of the homes before occupancy.

Before the Committee was a report by the
Corporate Director for Resources, copies of which had been
circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to the
signed copy of these minutes as Item 10.
 
The Fair, Green & Local Strategy was
presented to the Joint Strategic Committee in October 2025,
providing a clear framework for delivering priority programmes and
projects through Vesting Day for the new unitary authority in April
2028. The report recognised that the delivery plan would need to
evolve as the requirements of local government reorganisation
became clearer.
 
Since then, the local government reform
programme has progressed, with the decision on unitary footprints
now expected from the Secretary of State during July 2026. Local
elections had taken place, new administrations had been
established and significant progress had
been made towards the creation of the Sussex & Brighton
Strategic Authority, which held its first Annual General Meeting on
1 July 2026. As this work developed, further opportunities and
responsibilities were expected to emerge for local authorities
across Sussex.
 
Throughout this period of change, the
councils' focus on delivering high-quality frontline services and
supporting places would remain key, alongside a significant LGR
transition programme. In their annual speeches, both Leaders
emphasised a shared commitment to Pride in Place - delivering the
basics well through clean, safe and green town centres and
neighbourhoods, alongside supporting regeneration, economic
development and thriving local economies. Recognising both the
outstanding work of frontline teams and the significant financial
pressures facing local government, the Leaders also highlighted the
importance of strong partnership working with communities,
businesses and public sector partners to deliver the greatest
impact.
 
Pride in Place would become a cross-cutting
principle shaping/informing service
delivery, regeneration, environmental improvement, economic
development and partnership working. Alongside preparing for local
government reorganisation, it would ensure the councils continued
to deliver visible improvements to our places while positioning
Adur and Worthing to maximise opportunities for future investment,
government funding and sustainable growth.
 
Over 18 months there were opportunities to
strengthen operational collaboration with partners, particularly
West Sussex County Council, helping to build the integrated ways of
working that will be required under the future unitary
authority.
 
Over the summer, working closely with both
administrations, the Chief Executive would lead a further review of
the Fair, Green & Local delivery work programme. This would
sharpen the council's focus on Pride in Place while considering the
opportunities presented by the Sussex & Brighton Strategic
Authority and the evolving local government reform programme.
Engagement with communities and business would be an ongoing part
of this. A refreshed strategy would be presented in September,
setting out how Adur and Worthing Councils would position
themselves to maximise the opportunities presented by devolution,
secure external funding and investment, and deliver the greatest
benefit for residents, businesses and communities during the
transition.
 
Across the five mission areas, project
delivery is progressing well. Thriving Together had moved into
funded community action. Place and Environmental Services was
preparing for food waste collections and cleaner fleet changes.
Regeneration was progressing major coastal, town centre and asset
projects. Housing and Prevention had strengthened work on
homelessness prevention and Temporary Accommodation. Resource
Management was helping the councils prepare for Local Government
Reorganisation while continuing to support staff and services
 
 
Decision:
 

1.    
That progress on delivery of the Fair, Green & Local Corporate
Strategy and how it is being implemented across the five mission
areas be noted.
 

2.    
That mitigations to the projects assessed as amber (progress with
delays) and red (significant delays) be agreed.
 

3.    
That the assurance the Councils have put in place to ensure
oversight of delivery be noted. 
 

4.    
That the intention to further review the strategy and bring a
revised version forward in September, reflecting the focus on
“Pride in Place”, the LGR work programme and the
opportunities of devolution be noted 
 
 
Call In: The call-in deadline for
decisions will be 5.00pm on 23 July 2026.

Before the Committee was a report by the
Corporate Director for Resources, copies of which had been
circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to the
signed copy of these minutes as Item 6.
 
A new financial strategy was adopted in July
2024 and had played a significant role in stabilising the
medium term financial position of both
councils. It provided the foundation for discussion with MHCLG with
respect to the successful request for exceptional funding support
for Worthing. The strategy before members had not fundamentally
changed and the report before members showed how the organisation
would adapt to meet challenges.
 
The recent outturn reports showed that the
underlying financial challenges of two small ‘lower
tier’ authorities were still present, with housing need
continuing to be a significant factor for Worthing in particular.
It was expected that exceptional funding support would again be
needed for Worthing whilst underlying funding formula issues meant
that central funding continued to be insufficient to bridge the
financial gap.
 
The combined effects of long term funding shortfalls and a difficult
economic climate made the operating context for Local Government
extremely challenging. Despite this, both councils continued to
deliver successful local services and ambitious projects which were
focused on the long term visions of Adur
and Worthing.
 
Devolution and Local Government reorganisation
was welcomed in this context, not because it alone will ‘fix
the funding’ but because it was time to reinvent a system
which was under very significant ongoing pressure.
 
The timetable for this process would see a new
unitary council, of which Adur and Worthing would be part of,
coming into being in 2027 with full transfer of power and assets
(‘vesting’) in 2028. The strategy had therefore been
developed with that in mind in order to
continue to deliver on the responsibilities and priorities of Adur
and Worthing while also preparing the organisation for this
transition.
 
The joint “Fair, Green and Local
Plan” strategic framework would continue to be used to
support the delivery of both Administration's priorities, and was
supported by the councils’ financial strategy, designed to
provide a stable funding environment aligned to those priorities,
maintaining core service delivery and managing key risks.
 
 
Decision:
 

1.    
That the report and the outline 5 year
forecasts at appendix 1 be noted
 

2.    
That the updated financial strategy be approved, including the core
principles to support budget development.
 

3.    
That approval of the Financial Strategy for 2026/27 be recommended
to the Councils for approval

Before the Committee was a report by the
Service Director for Operations and Environmental Services, copies
of which had been circulated to all Members and a copy of which is

The Local Air Quality Management Framework
established by the Environment Act 1995 sets local limits for air
quality and requires local authorities to assess the quality of the
air in their district against objective, health-based levels. If
exceedances are identified, an Air Quality Management Area (AQMA)
must be declared and an action plan produced.
 
The two AQMA’s in Southwick and Shoreham
were revoked in December 2023 following a prolonged period of
compliance with the National Air Quality Objectives and a direction
from Defra to revoke the Shoreham High Street AQMA
 
The Government’s Air Quality Strategy
(2023) requires that local authorities without a declared AQMA must
develop and publish a local Air Quality Strategy, setting out
action the Council will take to improve air quality in their
area.
 
The report before Members reported the
findings of a public consultation for the new Air Quality Strategy
in Adur. The committee was asked to consider and approve the final
Adur Air Quality Strategy
 
Decision:
 

1.    
That the final Adur Air Quality Strategy be endorsed
 

2.    
That Adur District Council be recommended to approve the Adur Air
Quality Strategy

Before the Committee was a report by the
Service Director for Operations and Environmental Services, copies
of which had been circulated to all Members and a copy of which is
attached to the signed copy of these minutes as Item 14.
 
The report before Members addressed increasing
concerns regarding the negative impacts of excessive and
unregulated feeding of wildlife, particularly birds, in public
spaces within Worthing Town Centre, particularly in Montague Street
and around the Montague Quarter. Its purpose was to consider
implementation of a Public Space Protection Order (PSPO) within a
defined geographical area, or other options to mitigate issues
centred on public health, hygiene, and the degradation of public
realm caused by the resulting large wildlife populations and
fouling.
 
Members noted that there had been opposition
to the introduction of a PSPO in the consultation carried out.
However it was clear that there had been
negative impacts and local businesses had expressed concerns. It
was agreed that it was not currently appropriate to introduce a
PSPO, Members agreed that alternative options should be sought
 
Decision:
 

1.    
That concerns relating to the impacts of
the number of birds feeding and roosting, particularly in Montague
Street and around the Montague Quarter be acknowledged.
 

2.    
That it be noted that formal warnings and notices have been issued
to landlords of some of the properties that make up the Montague
Quarter to address issues of birds roosting and cleanliness on
their land.
 

3.    
That the consultation responses  be acknowledged and the strong opposition
to the implementation of a PSPO for wildlife feeding in the town
centre be noted.
 

4.    
That the implementation of a PSPO be not proceeded with.
 

5.    
That authority be delegated to the Service Director for Operations
and Environmental 
Services to consider implement alternatives in consultation
with the Cabinet Member for Environment.
 
Call In: The call-in deadline for
decisions will be 5.00pm on 23 July 2026.
topline: The Joint Strategic Committee has decided to not implement a Public Space Protection Order (PSPO) to address the negative impacts of excessive wildlife feeding in Worthing Town Centre.

decision_maker: Adur Cabinet Member for Economy and Regeneration
content:
To agree to the publication of the Draft Adur
Validation Requirements for consultation.
 
Note a further report will be submitted to
approve the final Adur Validation Requirements,following the
consultation.

The National Planning Policy Framework
requires local planning authorities to maintain and regularly
review their validation requirements. Publishing the draft document
for consultation will ensure that Adur District Council meets these
requirements while allowing applicants, planning agents, statutory
consultees and other stakeholders the opportunity to comment before
the document is finalised. The updated Validation Requirements will
improve the clarity and consistency of planning submissions, reduce
delays caused by invalid applications and support a more efficient
planning service.

Not undertaking public consultation was
considered but rejected. Consultation represents best practice,
provides an opportunity to improve the document through stakeholder
feedback and helps ensure the final Validation Requirements are
robust, proportionate and fit for purpose. Retaining the existing
Validation Requirements without review was also rejected as this
would not meet the expectation that local validation lists are
reviewed regularly and updated to reflect current legislation and
guidance.
topline: The Adur Cabinet Member for Economy and Regeneration has decided to publish the Draft Adur Validation Requirements for consultation.

decision_maker: Adur Cabinet Member for Economy and Regeneration, Worthing Cabinet Member for Economy and Regeneration
content:
To note the contents of this report and
authorise the Service Director for Place & Economy to place an
order for works under an existing Measured Terms Contract with JT
Mackleys & Co Ltd.
 
To authorise the Service Director for Place
and Economy to enter into a contract with HOP Consulting Ltd.
 
To note the financial section of this report
and note that estimates for the value of both contracts are circa
£550,000.00.
 
To note the matters which may cause the
estimated contract sums to vary and to further authorise a
variation to the estimated contract sum if it becomes necessary
based on reasonable evidence and supporting documentation,
providing the variation is in consultation with the Cabinet Members
and within the approved capital budget.

WBC Cabinet Member
for Economy & Regeneration:
Worthing Pier is one of our town's most
important heritage assets and an iconic part of our seafront. It
plays a central role in Worthing's coastal heritage, supports our
local economy, is home to successful local businesses and is
enjoyed by thousands of residents and visitors every year. The
temporary repair following the structural damage in 2024 ensured
the pier could safely remain open, but it was always intended as a
temporary solution. It is now right that we move forward with a
permanent repair and I am satisfied that the recommended approach
provides the best balance of engineering, heritage, value for money
and practical considerations, while ensuring the works can be
delivered within the approved capital budget.
 
ADC Cabinet Member
for Economy & Regeneration:
Although Worthing Pier is a Worthing Borough
Council asset, it is an important heritage landmark and a
significant contributor to the wider visitor economy shared across
Adur and Worthing. I welcome the careful work undertaken to
identify a permanent engineering solution following the temporary
repairs completed in 2024. Having considered the report, I am
satisfied that the recommended approach provides a robust and
deliverable long-term solution which protects this important
heritage asset, supports local businesses and visitors, and
represents an appropriate use of the approved capital budget.

WBC Cabinet Member
for Economy & Regeneration:
I considered the alternative repair options
set out in the report, together with the option of delaying a
decision while further work was undertaken. Having considered the
advice and evidence presented, I am satisfied that the recommended
solution provides the most appropriate and deliverable long term repair. Delaying the works would
unnecessarily prolong reliance on a temporary repair and defer the
long term protection of Worthing
Pier.
 
ADC Cabinet Member
for Economy & Regeneration:
I have considered the alternative repair
options and the option of delaying implementation. On balance, I
support the recommended approach as the most appropriate means of
securing the long-term future of Worthing Pier while avoiding
unnecessary reliance on the existing temporary structure.
topline: The Adur and Worthing Cabinet Members for Economy & Regeneration have decided to authorize contracts for permanent repairs to Worthing Pier, a key heritage asset and economic driver, with estimated costs of £550,000.00.

decision_maker: Service Director for Operations & Environmental Services (CLT)
content:
To award a contract to Combustion Solutions
Ltd (CSL) in the sum of £59,870.00 plus Vat to replace the
life expired analysers on the cremation plant.

These analysers provide the flue gas O2 &
CO readings to satisfy the requirements of the guidance notes
PG/5.  It is a legal requirement to
provide these reports on a monthly basis and forms part of the
council's permit to cremate.
 
The council has obtained a single quote from
Combustion Solutions Ltd who are the incumbent service and
maintenance contractor, and the only company approved in the UK by
DFW, the manufacturer of the cremators at Worthing Crematorium. If
an alternative supplier was used for this work, there would be a
split responsibility creating potential liability issues if there
are problems with the reporting data in the future i.e.one
organisation placing the responsibility on the other. For these
reasons it is recommended that the replacement of the analysers is
undertaken by CSL to ensure continuity of service and a single
point of responsibility.
 
The council’s existing capital programme
has a budget of £85K including fees that will cover the total
project cost with fees of £67,054.40 plus VAT.

There are very few alternative options as
there is a legal requirement to provide the correct O2 and CO
readings on a monthly basis.
 
Seeking alternative quotes given the
specialist nature of this work has been discounted for the reasons
given above.
topline: The Service Director for Operations & Environmental Services has decided to award a contract to Combustion Solutions Ltd to replace the analysers on the cremation plant.

content:
This decision proposes to vary the existing
MRI Housing System Contract to incorporate the MRI Community Safety
Platform. The current contract with MRI runs until April 2030, we
are proposing to sign the contract with a start date of 1 August
2026.
 
The total cost of the MRI Community Safety
Platform per annum is £17.8k, which equates to a total cost
of £65.2k over the remaining years of the contract.

Our current approach to managing Anti-Social
Behaviour (ASB) is split across two separate departments: the
Tenancy Services team and the Community Safety team. These teams do
not share a common platform for recording interactions or tracking
case progress. Consequently, officers are forced to store
information across fragmented Google Drive folders and
spreadsheets.
 
Furthermore, tenants currently have no
dedicated platform to report ASB directly. Reports must be made via
the contact centre or through email, both of which are only
monitored during standard business hours. This creates a
significant barrier for residents reporting incidents in real
time.
 
The existing housing management system lacks
the functionality required for robust case management; it cannot
ensure that ASB cases are documented in a format that can be
seamlessly exported into a legal case file. This disjointed process
hinders accountability and makes data collection or analysis nearly
impossible.
 
In recognition that our current approach to
management of ASB is insufficient and that we incorporated the
option to purchase this Antisocial Behaviour and Domestic Abuse
case management MRI Safer Communities within the existing Housing
System contract in 2025. We therefore propose we exercise our right
to access this platform within our contract
 
The MRI Community Safety Platform will:
 

1.   
Better support our community - It will make our
service available at all times with a self-service
portal.

2.   
Save time & resources - It consolidates all our case management
data into one comprehensive system to save time and improve our
team’s workflow.

3.   
Meet changing sector requirements - We will have confidence we are
investing in a solution that will be as useful tomorrow as it is
today.

No other option has been considered as we are
in contract with the current provider to deliver the digital
housing system until 2030. The option to vary our contract to
access the Community Safety Platform was incorporated within our
current contract.
topline: The Head of Policy, Performance & Strategy has decided to incorporate the MRI Community Safety Platform into the existing housing system contract to better manage Anti-Social Behaviour and improve case management.

impact the project would have on the cultural and creative sector
was outlined as well as the rationale for ADC to accept the grant
funding offer, work in partnership with the Ropetackle Centre Trust
and deliver the project and assume delegated authority for the
project related expenditure.

take on the overall responsibility of the improvement work at

Before the Committee was a report by the
Service Director for Place and Economy, copies of which had been
circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to the
signed copy of these minutes as Item 9.
 
The report before the Committee recommended
the process for the future of the asset at 30 Woods Way and
detailed that the asset was an industrial / warehouse property that
was held for investment purposes and had recently been taken back
from receivers following tenant failure. The report outlined that
the cost of refurbishment or redevelopment could not be met by
Worthing Borough Council (WBC), however, property of that type was
in demand for local businesses to provide expansion space, possibly
through redevelopment.
 
It was proposed that the property be placed on
the market for a freehold or long leasehold disposal with the sale
receipts being put into the General Fund.
 
Decision:
 

1.    
That the sale plan for the site be approved and the Service
Director for Place & Economy be authorised to progress with the
process. This includes proceeding with placing the property on the
market, through external commercial agents, to find a buyer,
negotiate and effect a sale.
 

2.    
That authority be delegated to the Service Director for Place and
Economy, to market the property and invite freehold and long
leasehold bids from the market which may include consideration of
social value that may be derived from the proposed sale. Members
will subsequently be consulted on the final selection of a
purchaser.
 

3.    
That it be noted that the property requires extensive repair and
investment and may be more valuable as a development opportunity.
It be agreed that the expression of interest exercise and
consequential sale contract may be on a ‘subject to
planning’ basis.
 

4.    
That authority be delegated to the Service Director for Place &
Economy to agree the Heads of Terms and to complete the sale
contract (or a lease) and any Contracts necessary in relation to
legal or consultancy services required, in consultation with the
Leader and Cabinet Member for Resources
 
 
Call In: The call-in deadline for
decisions will be 5.00pm on 19 June 2026.

being Fair, Green and Local. Good, safe and sustainable homes were
essential to enabling the Council's tenants to live and thrive in
Adur.
 
The report before members marked the move to
Phase Two of the Improvement Programme, focusing on all four of the
Consumer Standards and being "Inspection Ready" for the Regulator
of Social Housing. It sought approval for resources, for the
purposes of improving systems, data and programme change
capacity.
 
Officers had conducted a self-assessment
against all four of the Consumer Standards and had prepared a
Mock-Inspection using external assurance. Critical infrastructure
was required to ensure that Adur Homes was fully compliant.
 
Members were asked to approve existing
resources for the purposes of:
 
A Digital Housing System, to address business
critical issues regarding systems and data, which includes business
and data analytics support to identify business needs and to
develop key system processes;
An additional Community Safety Platform as
part of the system, to ensure compliance with the requirements in
relation to the management of Anti-Social Behaviour and Domestic
Abuse;
An extension of temporary Programme Change
capacity until April 2027
 
 
Decision:
 

1.    
That the highlighted progress made in relation to improving Adur
Homes and plans for the next phase of the Programme be noted.
 

2.    
That the virement be approved of £340,000 from the Adur Homes
Kitchens and Bathrooms capital budget to fund the new Digital
Housing System and the Community Safety Digital Platform, including
the Business and Data Analytics Support.
 

3.    
That the draw down of £17,800 revenue funding be approved
from the Housing Revenue Account Business Improvement Reserve for
the purposes of the annual license agreement for the Community
Safety Digital Platform for 2026/27. Noting that for year two
(2027/8) of the annual license agreement for the Community Safety
Digital Platform, revenue costs of £17,800 will be reprofiled
within the HRA, ensuring that costs remain within budget.
 

4.    
That the draw down of £76,000 be approved from the Housing
Revenue Account Business Improvement Reserve to extend the interim
Programme Change Manager from 1 August 2026 to 31 March 2027 to
ensure phase two of the programme is developed.
 

5.    
That the use of the Housing Revenue Account Business Improvement
Reserve fund of up to £190,000 into the general HRA budget be
approved, for the purposes of any other future transformation
requirements, arising from the Mock Inspection, to support
regulatory compliance, delegating any approved use of this to the
Corporate Director for Housing and Communities, in consultation
with the Cabinet Member for Housing and the Section 151
Officer.
 

6.    
That it be noted that the Corporate Director for Housing &
Communities will bring a detailed overview of our phase 1 position
and planned activity to the Joint Audit and Governance Committee in
June 2026.
 
 
Call In: The call-in deadline for
decisions will be 5.00pm on 19 June 2026.
