decision_maker: Adur Cabinet Member for Economy and Regeneration
content:
That the Cabinet Member:
 
a) notes the consultation responses received
in relation to: the Adur Green Infrastructure SPD; the Biodiversity
Net Gain Technical Advice Note the Urban Greening Technical Advice
Note
 
b) notes the officer consideration of
representations as set out within Appendix A – Consultation
Response Schedule
 
c) approves the amendments identified within
Appendix B – Schedule of Amendments Following
Consultation
 
d) adopts the Adur Green Infrastructure
SPD
 
e) jointly adopts with Worthing Borough
Council: the Biodiversity Net Gain Technical Advice Note; the Urban
Greening Technical Advice Note
 
f) authorises publication of the adopted
documents and associated consultation material.
 
g) delegates authority to the Head of Planning
to make any minor, non-material, editorial, typographical,
formatting, grammatical, cross-referencing and presentational
amendments to the adopted documents and supporting appendices prior
to publication, provided that such amendments do not materially
alter the substance, intent or policy position of the
documents.

The Adur Green Infrastructure and Biodiversity
Supplementary Planning Document (SPD), together with the
Biodiversity Net Gain Technical Advice Note and Urban Greening
Technical Advice Note, provide important guidance to support the
implementation of adopted planning policies relating to green
infrastructure, biodiversity, biodiversity net gain, urban
greening, trees and sustainable drainage systems.
 
The documents have been subject to public
consultation and have been amended in response to representations
received. The amendments improve clarity, usability and consistency
with adopted planning policy while maintaining the purpose of the
documents as guidance rather than introducing new policy
requirements. The SPD and Technical Advice Notes will support the
consistent, transparent and proportionate assessment of planning
applications, assist applicants in preparing development proposals,
and contribute to the delivery of biodiversity enhancement, climate
resilience, sustainable drainage, urban greening and wider
environmental objectives across Adur.

Option 1 – Not
adopt the documents.
This option was rejected as it would result in
the absence of up-to-date planning guidance to support the
implementation of adopted Local Plan policies relating to green
infrastructure, biodiversity and biodiversity net gain. This could
reduce consistency in decision-making and provide less certainty
for applicants and decision-makers.
 
Option 2 –
Undertake further consultation and defer adoption.
This option was considered unnecessary as the
documents have already been subject to public consultation and the
representations received have been carefully considered.
Appropriate amendments have been made where necessary and officers
are satisfied that the documents are suitable for adoption.
topline: The Adur Cabinet Member for Economy and Regeneration has decided to adopt the Adur Green Infrastructure and Biodiversity Supplementary Planning Document, along with related technical advice notes, to support sustainable development and environmental objectives.

content:
Award contract for 2 plus 1 years to My Money
Matters (MMM) for an estimated value of £25,000* per annum.
There is a 5% charge applicable which is invoiced against the total
monthly contributions. The cost for this will be marginal as it is
dependent on the number of members. *It has been identified that
the cost associated with SCAVCs is likely to be offset against the
Employer National Insurance (NI) savings

The LGPS has a provision within its
regulations to allow an employer to also contribute to an
employee’s AVC arrangement. This is known as a ‘Shared
Cost’ AVC which can be provided through a salary sacrifice
arrangement. A salary sacrifice arrangement is a popular and
legitimate method used by employers to provide employees with a
benefit.
 
By doing so this will boost the
Council’s employee benefit scheme and allow further savings
to both the Councils Employer and Employee National Insurance
Contributions (NICs), especially significant since the Employer NI
% inflation and threshold decrease in April 2025. The scheme offers
employees an opportunity for efficient retirement planning, and
similar schemes already operate successfully across many other
authorities.

It is not possible to operate this type of
scheme under self admin. It is only LGPS standard AVCs which are
currently operated in house by the Payroll team. However standard
AVCs do not provide the additional benefits of Employer and
Employee NI savings. My Money Matters (MMM) is the only company
that operates and manages this scheme.
topline: The Assistant Director Finance has decided to award a contract to My Money Matters for an employee benefit scheme involving Shared Cost AVCs to boost savings on National Insurance contributions.

content:
A Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service
is a cybersecurity service that combines technology with human
expertise to rapidly identify and limit the impact of threats by
performing threat hunting, monitoring, and response. The main
benefit of MDR is that it quickly helps in limiting the impact of
threats without the need for additional staffing.
 
The current contract for supplying an MDR
service will end on 28/06/2026. The intention is not to renew with
the incumbent supplier and take out a new one year direct award
contract with Nomios, who offer better
value for money and a more mature offering. 
 
The value of the 12-month contract is
£71,000 + VAT

Security is at the forefront of Digital and
this decision is based on the ongoing need for advanced
cybersecurity measures to protect against evolving threats. This
new contract will continue to show the value of MDR in rapidly
identifying and mitigating cyber threats without requiring
additional staffing. The move to Nomios
should provide a better service, safeguarding critical systems and
data, while ensuring cost-efficiency.

Do nothing and let the current contract expire
without putting an alternative solution in-place, introducing a
cost saving. This was discounted as the risk in not monitoring our
environment is too great.
 
 
Extend the MDR service with the
current  supplier. This was also
discounted for predominantly two reasons. Firstly the existing
service has been delivered adequately but hasn’t seen service
or technical improvements. Secondly the cost of the proposed
solution is more cost effective.
topline: The Head of Technology & Design has decided to award a new one-year contract for a Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service to Nomios for better value and cybersecurity measures.

content:
The Council continues to use Zurich Municipal

independent broker. Zurich Municipal have provided cover for the

Worthing Pier.
 
The premium paid of £101k per annum
covers for fire, lightning, explosion and aircraft (FLEA) at an
indemnity of £5m. This level of cover and premium is
comparable with industry standard for an asset like Worthing Pier.
This decision would ensure that Zurich Municipal covered Worthing
Pier for the period from 1st June 2026 to 31st May 2028.

The current insurance for the Pier expires on

The Council went through an independent broker

full reinstatement cover. Only two companies put forward a quote
with the alternative putting forward an annual premium that far
exceeded the budget the Council has available to provide insurance
cover for Worthing Pier.

content:
The approved planning consented flood defence
design adjacent to Sussex Yacht Club in Shoreham requires the
implementation of joint operational procedure agreed between Adur
District Council and Sussex Yacht Club for the management of the
flood gates once construction of the development has been
completed.
 
This decision is for Adur District Council to
enter into an agreement with Sussex Yacht Club (SYC) for the
management and operation of two Flood Gates that will be installed
as part of the Flood Defence construction project adjacent to SYC
and Brighton Road in Shoreham. This agreement sets out the terms of
the management of the Flood Gates.  

Adur District Council (ADC) will hold the
overall ownership, liability and maintenance responsibility of the
flood defences, including issuing the instruction to close flood
gates. However, this Flood Gates Management Plan adds greater
resilience through partnering with the Sussex Yacht Club (SYC) who
will use their own team of local, trained volunteers for the
physical operation to allow for quicker deployment based on
minute-by-minute tidal information - and to allow them to operate
and maintain access to their site right up to the event occurring
and shortly after it has passed, minimising any potential
disruption to the yacht club and its members access.
 
The Flood Gates Management Plan will ensure
suitable procedures and processes are in place to support the
ongoing management of the flood defences.
 

Other agencies were approached to manage the
flood gates, including the Environment Agency, however they were
unable to commit to the resources. Therefore, it was considered
necessary to prepare an operational management plan which was
practical and agreeable for all parties involved (ADC and SYC),
with the emphasis being on reaction speed to mitigate against flood
events.
 
ADC briefly considered being the sole
operator, but this wouldn’t practically work with SYC as the
gates would likely be sealed the day before a flood event and
opened the day after, meaning access and disruption for the SYC
could be impacted unnecessarily.
 
Other Matters
Considered: 
 
A key focus has been addressing liability, as
SYC is not able to hold any responsibility should the gates fail.
The Council's insurance has been confirmed to cover volunteers,
provided they are under the Council’s control and
appropriately trained. The final management plan has been prepared
in full consultation with SYC. 
 
This final protocol includes details on
operator training (provided by the contractor, Flood Control
International) and a communication system for alerts and
confirmations. The Flood Gates Management Plan has now been
produced and will be ready for implementation and operation once
the flood defences have been completed.
topline: The Chief Executive has decided to enter into an agreement with Sussex Yacht Club for the management and operation of flood gates in Shoreham.

This decision directly awards HQN (Housing
Quality Network) the contract of leading an external assurance
exercise. The cost of this commission is £24900, but HQN have
projected a further £1500 in expenses, taking the total cost
to be £26400.

This commission of HQN (Housing Quality
Network) provides a high quality advice, tailored support and
training provider for housing associations to deliver an external
assurance process which is fundamental for the Adur Homes
Improvement Programme. We expect to receive constructive challenges
and support through this process that will enable us to improve our
homes. This assessment process will help us to prepare for the
Regulator's Inspection.
 
At the end of the exercise, HQN will provide a
PowerPoint presentation summarising their findings, including
commentary on:
 

-       
The robustness of our approach to document submission and
supporting evidence.

-       
Our areas of strength, as well as those requiring further
investigation or action —including, where relevant, any
potential “showstoppers” or topics suitable for deep
dives.

-       
An indicative consumer standard rating — and the rationale
behind it.

-       
Feedback on our presentation, with suggestions for improvement.

-       
Their views on our action plan — including comments on its
scope, priorities, timescales, and any gaps.

-       
Their prioritised recommendations, which can be used to help revise
our improvement plan.

-       
Suggestions for how we could enhance our current approach or
strengthen the evidence base.

-       
Feedback on the interviews and meetings — including practical
suggestions to improve responses or presentation.

-       
Their views and recommendations on the organisation and
housekeeping of the inspection process, including confidential
feedback on individual interviews if appropriate.
 
The cost of this inspection is £24,900k
inc VAT.
 
HQN also expects there to be a maximum of
£1.5k in expenses

We are not aware of other Providers offering
this service and this Provider has a track record nationally of
offering an external assurance service to a number of registered
providers.
 
This external process will complement steps we
are taking internally as part of our self-assessment.

decision_maker: Adur Cabinet Member for Housing and Citizen Services
content:
I approve the decision to enter into contracts
with the preferred three contractors (Ecosafe Heating Limited, HMG
Building Services and GDM Building Solutions) described in this
report to deliver the Southwick Voids Refurbishment programme and
approve a total budget of £2 million to refurbish these 44
void properties.

Bringing empty homes back into use for
residents is a key priority for this administration. The three
preferred contractors provide the strongest combination of
expertise and value for money, while also helping to distribute
workload and risk to ensure properties are completed and ready for
tenancy as quickly as possible. This approach will help reduce both
the housing waiting list and reliance on costly, and often
unsuitable, temporary accommodation, while also restoring rental
income. All three contractors already have an established presence
in West Sussex.

Direct award of the contract to a large
national contractor through a compliant framework agreement was
considered; however, Adur Homes’ relatively small housing
stock made this option uncompetitive. An open or staged competitive
procurement process was also discounted due to the anticipated
timescales of 9–12 months.
topline: The Adur Cabinet Member for Housing and Citizen Services has decided to approve contracts with three preferred contractors to refurbish 44 void properties in Southwick.

content:
To appoint the following services to support
the flood defence scheme:
 
Mark Guthrie Anderson Consultants (MGAC)
serves as the Council's Quantity Surveyor and Project Management
support for the Shoreham Flood Defences development. Their
responsibilities include cost analysis and pricing, procurement and
contractor selection, drafting the NEC4 construction contract,
liaison and project managing the implementation of the construction
contractors delivery programme, and
reporting to the client (ADC) on construction progress. This
service is required up to project completion. This is at a cost of
£58,752 (excluding VAT).
 
Hemsley Orrell Partnership (HOP) Consulting
are the project's Design/Engineering Consultants. They are
responsible to act as principal designer (under CDM 2015 and
Building Regulations 2022) providing technical competence, relevant
construction experience, and the capability to manage
pre-construction health and safety risks, producing drawings and
specifications for the construction contractor. This detailed
design work involves progressing the scheme to the RIBA 4 Work
stages (detailed design) in readiness to tender and appoint
construction contractors. Their knowledge and advice will be
required beyond this stage, likely on an ad-hoc basis, up to the
point of project completion. This is at a cost of £47,900
(excluding VAT).
 
Both sets of figures are contained within the
financial envelope for these services to support the construction
of the flood wall.

Adur District Council does not have the
available resources in-house to be able to design and/or manage
this project directly, therefore due to the significance of the
scheme, professional services are required.

MGAC and HOP have both been working on the
project from RIBA Workstages 1-4. If
the Council were to go with any other providers at this point, this
is likely to create delays and additional costs to the project.
topline: The Chief Executive has decided to appoint external consultants to support the flood defence scheme in Shoreham.

content:
To appoint Blanchard Wells construction
contractor to deliver the Flood Defences adjacent to Sussex Yacht
Club in Shoreham for the maximum budget threshold value as set out
in the exempt appendix to the JSC report and agreed by Members at
the JSC meeting on 9 December 2025.
 
The appointment of a construction contractor
is necessary to deliver the Shoreham Flood Defences project, which
includes the construction of the main flood wall and gates,
pathway, associated piling, surfacing works, and drainage. This
work is a crucial flood defences scheme to protect properties
adjacent to the A259 Brighton Road to the north and Sussex Yacht
Club (SYC) to the south. The construction programme will commence
this summer with an anticipated winter 2026 finish, with the total
programme for mobilisation and delivery estimated at 34 weeks. The
location is considered as being at risk of surface water flooding
with flooding taking place in 2025, highlighting the critical need
for the new flood defence defences.

Following a full procurement process Blanchard
Wells will be appointed as the preferred contractor. The decision
was based on the set tender scoring criteria of 70% price and 30%
quality. Blanchard Wells scored 92% in the tender and has a wealth
of experience in delivering coastal construction projects.

The contract was formally tendered, therefore
other bids considered were not viable  -
Adur District Council (ADC) are not specialised to undertake this
work “in-house”.
topline: The Chief Executive has decided to appoint Blanchard Wells construction contractor to deliver flood defences in Shoreham.

decision_maker: Deputy CEO & Corporate Director for Housing & Communities
content:
To enter into a Service Level Agreement with
West Sussex County Council for the delivery of the Adur &
Worthing Connect to Work Programme, in accordance with the terms of
the Department for Work and Pensions grant funding, for the period
April 2026 to April 2030.

The decision enables the Council to formally
participate in the Connect to Work programme which is a national
scheme designed to deliver and deliver locally tailored employment
support to economically inactive residents.
 
The programme is fully funded through a
£521,615 grant from West Sussex County Council (funded by the
Department for Work and Pensions) and aligns with the
Councils’ priorities as Fair Councils in relation to Housing
and Prevention priorities, by supporting vulnerable residents,
improving wellbeing, and increasing economic participation.
 
Entering into the Service Level Agreement
ensures that the Council can meet the programme’s performance
and delivery requirements as set out by the accountable body, West
Sussex County Council.

The option of not entering into the Service
Level Agreement and therefore not delivering the programme was
considered.
 
This option was not recommended as it would
result in missed opportunities to support economically inactive
residents and would leave a gap in provision that existing services
are not resourced to fill. The programme provides a personalised,
integrated and sustained approach to employment support, including
in-work support, which is not available through existing
provision.
 
Declining the agreement would also mean the
Council would not benefit from the external grant funding available
to deliver these outcomes.
topline: The Deputy CEO & Corporate Director for Housing & Communities has decided to enter into a Service Level Agreement for the delivery of the Adur & Worthing Connect to Work Programme.

The Charges for Building Regulations work are

which is carried out for the benefit of a disabled person where
that work is charge exempt. There are two methods that the
Authority may use to establish the charge for building work, either
Standard Charges or Individually Determined Charges.

To ensure the Councils’ apply robust and
calculated fees and charges for Building Control Services in line
with national regulations.

To apply a standard rate for the services

resources implications and ability to perform said services. While

content:
Before the
Committee was a report by the Corporate Director for Housing and
Communities and Economy, copies of which had been circulated to all
Members and a copy of which is attached to the signed copy of these
minutes as Item 6.
 
The report before
the Committee sought formal approval to accept grant funding from
West Sussex County Council (WSCC), funded by the Department for
Work and Pensions (DWP), for the implementation of the Adur and
Worthing Connect to Work scheme.
 
Connect to Work was
a national scheme that was being rolled out in local areas, with
the purpose of providing tailored employment support for residents
to improve economic participation, wellbeing, and financial
resilience. 
 
The report proposed
that Adur and Worthing Councils locally delivered the programme
alongside some of the other Councils in West Sussex. The funding
proposal covered the timeframe from April 2026 until April 2030,
with the potential to extend the programme. 
 
As Fair
Councils’ the proposed programme would work alongside other
prevention programmes to provide dedicated help for residents
facing multiple barriers to employment and who were economically
inactive but wished to work. The Work was part of the Councils
housing and prevention work programme and functioned alongside
other services including going local
.


Decision: 


That the overall programme and its
contribution to prevention and support for vulnerable people be
noted;

 
2.  
That the DWP grant funding of £521,615.00 be approved and
accepted, from West Sussex County Council for a period of 4 years
commencing April 2026 until April 2030 to deliver the Connect to
Work scheme;
 
3.  
That a revenue budget to enable the delivery of the Connect to Work
Scheme, wholly funded from the DWP Connect to Work grant be
approved;
 
4.  
That the potential for extension after April 2030, subject to
funding conditions be noted;
 
5.  
That authority be delegated to the Corporate Director for Housing
and Communities, in consultation with the respective Cabinet
Members for Health and Wellbeing, to enter into a Service Level
Agreement for the purposes of delivering this programme. 


Call In: The call-in deadline for decisions will be 5.00pm
on 8 April 2026.

decision_maker: Service Director for Operations & Environmental Services (CLT)
content:
Letting of the contract for Adur District and
Worthing Borough Council’s stray dog service with
AlphaguardK9 Limited of Railway Lofts, 19c Commercial Road,
Eastbourne, BN21 3XE for an initial term of 2 years and optional
extensions of up to a total of 5 years from the 1st of April 2026.
Over 5 Years the total estimated value of the contract would be
£187,500.00

Adur and Worthing Councils
currently operate a dog warden service to collect, kennel and
process stray dogs which are reported through the councils contact
team or website. They operate across both councils but also provide
the service to Arun district council. In order to align with the
wider districts and boroughs ahead of LGR, alongside saving costs
the councils sought an external supplier to deliver the
service. 
 
The service area discussed the
requirement with procurement and determined a strategy to undertake
market research ahead of running an open tender process. The
contract will be split into 2 lots, one for Arun and another for
Adur and Worthing. Running for an initial period of 2 years with
optional extensions of up to three further years in annual
renewals. 
 
On the 16th of December the
council undertook a market testing exercise in line with the
guidance of The Procurement Act 2023. Officers released a
preliminary market engagement notice on the find a tender platform
with a closing date of the 12th of January 2026. 
 
The market testing exercise had
over 500 views but no expressions of interest were received
directly. 
 
On the 16th of January 2026
officers released the tender to the open market through a notice
published on the find a tender portal. The tenders deadline for
responses was the 16th of February 2026. The tender received no
view or interest within the first two weeks, officers contacted
every dog warden / dog collection service that we could identify
operating within Sussex and received little interest with only two
companies engaging with the tender.
 
Officers extended the tender to
allow the interested suppliers more time but only received a single
bid as of the 23rd of February 2026. Officers from all three
authorities evaluated the bid chaired by procurement concluding
that the supplier bidding was competent and the costs still
reflected a saving against the current costs of operating the
service. 
 
It is therefore recommended that
the contract move ahead with AlphaguardK9, based in Eastbourne
(they currently operate the same service for Eastbourne, Lewes and
Brighton council’s). 
 

Retaining the service in house has been
considered but it is significantly more expensive
topline: The Service Director for Operations & Environmental Services has decided to award the contract for Adur District and Worthing Borough Council's stray dog service to AlphaguardK9 Limited.

content:
That Worthing Borough Council to appoint
Bellrock as Managing Agent to oversee the management facilities and
NHS tenants of the Worthing Integrated Care Centre (WICC) on an
interim basis from 1 April to 1 July 2026, until such time a
permanent Managing Agent contract has been formally proposed and
recommended for approval through the Joint Strategic Committee.
 
Fees payable to Bellrock under the appointment
are collected by them from accrued Service Charge payments made by
the tenants of the building under the terms of their lease.

Savills had previously been appointed by the
Council to provide the managing agent requirements. Savills are
currently acting as managing agents for the WICC Building and were
originally brought into the management process for the building
because at that time the NHS tenants had not entered into a lease.
This responsibility was with the Council to fulfil through
Savills.
 
The reason for the change is, that in the
development of the Service Charge arrangements, Savills established
that the level of Health Technical Memoranda (HTM) requirements
necessary to serve the NHS services who will operate from the
building, is above and beyond what Savills are specialised to
perform.
 
The enhanced specialist compliant requirements
to operate a HTM compliant building to be provided by Bellrock
include:
 

·        
HTM governance

·        
Healthcare engineering expertise

·        
Enhance compliance reporting

·        
Infection control integration

·        
Critical infrastructure resilience

·        
Water treatment and monitoring

·        
Clinical waste handling
 
All necessary operational policies,
maintenance regimes, and audits align with the relevant HTMs.
 
Although Savills are fully versed in managing
large scale commercial buildings they do not offer the enhanced
level of structured competency and governance to facilitate the
important services to meet NHS estate governance requirements.
Therefore they will not be in a position to manage the day to day
management of the facility for the following:-
 
NHS Occupiers
 

·        
Sussex Community NHS Foundation Trust

·        
Sussex Partnership NHS Foundation Trust

·        
Worthing Medical Group

·        
Paydens
 
Bellrock are already engaged and familiar with
the property and have the specialised expertise to fulfil all
necessary HTM compliant services as part of a current consultancy
appointment. Whereby Bellrock has been working with Savills and the
NHS to ensure the WICC is ready to become fully operationalised at
the point issues associated with the water system are resolved.
 
The Council intends to appoint Bellrock for an
interim appointment as the managing agent to ensure continuity of
service for the management of the building is assured, while the
Council determines the longer term procurement requirements for a
formal Management Contract Award. As part of this contractual
appointment the existing Facility Manager with Savills’ who
holds the knowledge and experience of the building, will be TUPED
from Savills to Bellrock to support the ongoing management of the
building.

Managing HTM compliance requires specialist
Building Management expertise to facilitate and manage. Bellrock
will be appointed by the Council to undertake initial consultancy
services due to their knowledge of what is required in terms of
integrating NHS and health services. This is essential. There are
not adequate resources to fully procure alternative Building
Management services to commence by the beginning of April.
topline: The Service Director for Place & Economy has decided to appoint Bellrock as the interim Managing Agent for the Worthing Integrated Care Centre.

content:
To award grants totalling £60,000 from
the Thriving Together Fund as follows:
 

Adur Voluntary Action &
Community Works for Communities Together: £15,00
Esteem for Our Voice, Our Community:
£10,000
Community People for On Your
Doorstep: £12,500
Worthing Festival for Worthing
Festival & Fringe 2026: growing our town together:
£12,500
Sight Support Worthing for Training
understanding & support for sight loss: £10,000

 
An overview of these projects is below.
 
Funding will be paid in March 2026 in line
with the requirement that all funding be awarded within the 2025/26
financial year
 

The Thriving Together Fund forms part of the
wider Thriving Together programme, which supports community-led
action and neighbourhood collaboration across Adur and
Worthing.
 
The Fund was designed to:
 

Strengthen community cohesion
Build preventative, community-based
support
Reduce cost-of-living pressures
Grow collaboration and capability
within the local voluntary and community sector
 

The projects approved for funding were
assessed as those best able to:

Demonstrate meaningful collaboration
between groups
Deliver preventative and early help
activity
Reduce duplication and strengthen
joined-up local support
Provide value for money and
realistic delivery plans
Leave a practical legacy (e.g.
shared tools, training, approaches, or models) that other groups
can use or build on
 

The decision supports the Councils’
wider ambitions to build stronger, more connected
neighbourhoods.
 
The projects highlighted were assessed as
being the projects best able to build capability for local groups
while making the strongest positive impact on local communities and
leaving practical resources that others can use and benefit from,
and specifically those projects that best met the criteria
identified in the 
Scoring Guide.
 
The Thriving Together Fund forms part of the
wider Thriving Together programme and was co-designed with local
groups in October 2025.
 
The Fund guidance and FAQs were published in
advance on
 

https://participate.adur-worthing.gov.uk/en-GB/projects/thriving-together 
 

Thriving Together Grant Fund Guidance
 

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
 
A total of 48 eligible applications were
received.
 
Applications were:
 

Assessed against a scoring framework
aligned to the Fund criteria
Scored independently by panel
members
Moderated and validated through
structured panel discussions

 
The assessment structure was:
 

Adur Panel – proposals
delivering activity in Adur
Worthing Panel – proposals
delivering activity in Worthing
Joint Adur & Worthing Panel
– cross-boundary proposals and validation of highest scoring
projects

Panel membership included relevant Cabinet
Members and Neighbourhood Leads as well as input into the Panel
from service leads (Wellbeing, Safer Communities and
Proactive).
 
Scores were based on:
 

Impact through collaboration
Contribution to cost of living,
cohesion and/or prevention
Strengthening of local groups and
shared capability
Deliverability and value for
money
Practical legacy (shared tools,
models, training or approaches others can reuse)
 

Given the fixed budget envelope of
£60,000, prioritisation was required. Funding the highest
scoring projects ensures the greatest collective impact within
available resources.
 

All 48 eligible applications were
assessed.
 
Several applications demonstrated merit;
however, the available funding did not allow all proposals to be
supported.
 
Alternative options would have included:

Funding a larger number of smaller
projects
Allocating funding evenly regardless
of score

 
These options were not pursued as they would
have reduced the impact that the Fund was designed to
achieve 
 
Feedback will be offered to unsuccessful
applicants and learning on the trends in terms of needs and
capability building all projects wanted to respond to will be used
to inform the Thriving Together Fund for 2026/27.
topline: The Assistant Director for People & Change has decided to award grants totalling £60,000 from the Thriving Together Fund to support community-led projects in Adur and Worthing.

Before the Committee was a report by the
Service Director for Place & Economy, copies of which had been
circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to the
signed copy of these minutes as Item 16.
 
Following the insolvency of Adur Community
Leisure, South Downs Leisure (the Worthing leisure provider) were
appointed as an interim provider of leisure services in Adur
District while the Council carried out a review of how best to
deliver leisure services for both Adur and Worthing residents.
 
This report outlined the key considerations in
making the recommendation that the
longer term Adur Leisure Contract is
directly awarded to South Downs Leisure. There have been many
benefits to the residents of Adur and Worthing in having a mutual
provider which enables the public to access a greater variety of
facilities across Adur and Worthing.
 
Subject to Member authority, it was
operationally beneficial, to merge service delivery under these two
separate contracts, to form a new joint arrangement for a period of
21 years starting from 1st April 2026.
 
The report summarised the rationale and lawful
procurement route for recommending a direct award to South Downs
Leisure for the Adur leisure provision and asked members to
authorise the proposed recommendations based on the information
within this report.
 
Decision:
 

1.   
That South Downs Leisure be approved as the chosen provider to
operate the leisure facilities across Adur District Council on the
terms set out in this report and the Exempt Appendix and that
authority be delegated the Service Director for Place & Economy
to enter into a Funding and Management Agreement for Adur Leisure
delivery with South Downs Leisure.
 

2.   
That the Service Director for Place & Economy be authorised to
enter into the site leases which form
the collective Adur Leisure delivery on the heads of terms as set
out in the Exempt Appendix.
 

3.   
That it be agreed that the existing Worthing Borough Council
Funding & Management Agreement be varied to incorporate the
Adur Leisure Service Delivery, the term of both Adur and Worthing
Leisure delivery to terminate on 31st March 2047.
 

4.   
That it be agreed that the existing Worthing Leisure site leases be
extended to 31st March 2047 on the heads of terms which are set out
in the Exempt appendix.

5.   
That the Service Director for Place & Economy be authorised to
negotiate final terms, and to agree such variations as are required
to the Worthing Borough Council Funding & Management Agreement
to enable delivery of services as set out in the Head of Terms and
Exempt Appendix (or terms which substantially the same as or
similar to those terms), in the opinion of the Chief Financial
Officer, Leaders of Worthing and Adur Councils and Cabinet Members
for Leisure).
 

6.   
In the event that the terms vary for any reason and are not similar
to or substantially the same as those set out in the Exempt
Appendix, that authority be delegated to the Service Director for
Place & Economy in consultation with Chief Financial Officer,
Leaders of Worthing and Adur Councils and Cabinet Members for
Leisure to negotiate and authorise the necessary contractual
amendments and to complete the variation to the Funding &
Management Agreement, grant of site leases to South Downs Leisure,
and all legal documentation to facilitate delivery of leisure
services by South Downs Leisure from 1st April 2026.
 

7.   
That authority be delegated to the Service Director for Place &
Economy to make any variations to existing Worthing Borough Council
Leases as required to facilitate the Heads of Terms and Funding
& Management Agreement.
 

8.   
That authority be delegated to the Service Director for Place &
Economy authority to:-
 
a.   
Manage all operational aspects of the relationship between Adur and
Worthing Councils and South Downs Leisure on the terms set out in
the new and updated Funding and Management Agreement between SDL
and the Councils detailed in Section 7 subject always to regular
quarterly review meetings with South Downs Leisure which the
Cabinet Members for Leisure will be invited to attend.
 
b.   
Submit an annual report to the Joint Strategic Committee on the
performance of South Downs Leisure under the new contractual
arrangements.
 
 
Call In: The call-in deadline for
decisions will be 5.00pm on 13 March 2026.

Before the Committee was a report by the
Service Director for Operations & Environmental Services,
copies of which had been circulated to all Members and a copy of
which is attached to the signed copy of these minutes as Item

The Worthing Heat Network (WHN) project had
benefited from government Heat Network Infrastructure Project
(HNIP) funding during procurement, design and construction of Phase
1.
 
Hemiko, who were
responsible for the design, build, operation, and maintenance of
the network, had been granted planning permission for the next
phase of construction ‘Densification Phase 1’.
 
To minimise disruption associated with the
next phase of work a new construction methodology was being adopted
Horizontal Directional Drilling (HDD). HDD avoided the need for
open trench construction but is more expensive than traditional
open trench construction. Other project costs had also increased
significantly beyond inflation.
 
In addition to cost increases, the delay to
Heat Network Zoning was reducing the uptake of new connections to
the heat network.
 
In response to these challenges the report
sought approval to apply for further HNIP funding to contribute to
the capital costs of extending the heat network using HDD
technology and bringing forward the installation of a second air
source heat pump at the energy centre in readiness for future
connections.
 
Decision:
 

1.   
That authority be delegated to the Service Director for Operations
& Environmental Services to enter into a grant funding
agreement with Triple Point for receipt into Worthing Borough
Council’s budget the amount of £8.02 million grant
funding for the purposes of on-granting
to Hemiko for use as capital investment
in the next agreed phase of construction of the Worthing Heat
Network (Densification Phase 1).
 

2.   
That authority be delegated to the Service Director for Operations
& Environmental Services to on-grant the full amount of grant
funding to Hemiko pursuant to an

content:
Before the Committee was a report by the Chief
Executive, copies of which had been circulated to all Members and a
copy of which is attached to the signed copy of these minutes as
Item 11.
 
The report provided the 2026 annual update on
the Sussex Bay programme, building on the update presented to the
Joint Strategic Committee in February 2025.
 
Progress was outlined since the formal launch
of the programme in June 2024, including the publication of the
inaugural 2025 Annual Report and Blueprint for Seascape Recovery,
Part 1 (which forms the Sussex ‘voluntary’ marine
extension to the Local Nature Recovery Strategy), and the
anniversary event held in June 2025. It also provides an update on
delivery across the mission, three work packages, funding secured,
partnerships developed, outcomes achieved and next steps.
 
Sussex Bay was hosted by Adur & Worthing
Councils and operated both within and beyond their administrative
boundaries, working across the wider Sussex region from Camber
Sands to Selsey Bill. This area spans approximately 100 miles of
coastline and serves more than 1.7 million residents. While the
programme operates at a regional scale, much of its activity
delivers direct benefits for the communities within the host
Councils, supporting local environmental recovery, engagement and
place-based outcomes.
 
The Sussex Bay programme was forecast to
secure £2 million in non-Council funding by its second
anniversary in June 2026 since the launch in June 2024. Funding was
secured through competitive processes and awarded for clearly
defined, specific purposes linked to the programme mission.
 
Sussex Bay built upon many years of preceding
leadership by Adur and Worthing Councils in sustainability, nature
recovery and community-led work, strengthening and extending this
work through a coordinated, place-based approach that supports
long-term environmental, social and economic resilience.
 
Building upon the approach to-date, over the
proceeding year, it was planned to
pilot a targeted roll-out of a “Sussex Bay Champions”
approach, building on innovative work developed with colleagues
from Lewes and Eastbourne Councils. This would support a network of
community champions, providing training and guidance to enable
small-group conversations that help shape the Blueprint for
Seascape Recovery at a local level. The approach would carefully
manage expectations while encouraging meaningful participation, and
will align with the principles of the locally growing Generation
Restoration (Gen R) movement: nature and people first, positive,
collaborative and kind
 
Decision:
 
 

1.   
That the progress made by the Sussex Bay programme since the
previous update, February 2025 be noted.
 

2.   
That the continued development of Sussex Bay as a regional model
for marine, coastal and estuarine recovery be endorsed, delivered
through ongoing work under the Blueprint for Seascape Recovery, and
support the trial of the “Community Champions’
approach, funded through existing externally provided funding to
the Councils.
 

3.   
That the external funding that the Sussex Bay programme has
attracted to date be acknowledged and the headline and ring-fenced
areas for its expenditure be endorsed.
 

4.   
That the programme of future events be endorsed, including the
existing quarterly Members forum with Leaders from each of the 11
Councils in the Sussex Bay programme area whilst balancing the need
for ownership and the regional inclusivity.
 

5.   
That continued collaboration with partners, communities and
stakeholders across the Sussex Bay programme area be supported,
both within the administrative boundaries of Adur & Worthing
and outside.
 

6.   
That the intent to publish the 2026 annual report and Blueprint for
Seascape Recovery, Part 2 from June 2026 be approved, to coincide
with the programme’s second anniversary events and World
Oceans Day, and endorse further
community consultation later on in the
year.
 
Call In: The call-in deadline for
decisions will be 5.00pm on 13 March 2026.
topline: The Joint Strategic Committee has decided to endorse the continued development of the Sussex Bay programme for marine, coastal, and estuarine recovery.

decision_maker: Service Director for Operations & Environmental Services (CLT)
content:
To proceed with the collaborative project with
Magtec, utilizing Advanced Propulsion
Centre (APC) grant funding to repower a Council-owned Refuse
Collection Vehicle (RCV) with an electric driveline. This decision
approves the release of a donor vehicle for conversion, with the
unit scheduled to re-enter service by October. 
 
While the capital cost of the electric
driveline is fully grant-funded, the Council are required to commit
to a £13,000 per annum Repair and Maintenance (R&M)
contract to support the electric system once in service.  This
will be entered into for the next five years assuming the vehicle
remains in active service during this time.
 

This decision supports the Council’s
commitment to achieving Net Zero by accelerating the
decarbonization of its heavy goods fleet. Utilizing the Advanced
Propulsion Centre (APC) grant allows the Council to trial electric
RCV technology with minimal capital exposure, avoiding the
significant cost of purchasing a new electric vehicle (typically
exceeding £400,000). Furthermore, by repowering an existing
chassis and refurbishing the body, the Council adopts a circular
economy approach that extends the useful life of a Council asset,
reduces embodied carbon, and secures essential operational data to
inform future fleet procurement strategies.

The option to purchase a brand-new electric
RCV was considered but rejected due to the prohibitive capital cost
(typically over £400,000) compared to this grant-funded
repower opportunity. Additionally, the 'do nothing' approach of
continuing to operate the current diesel driveline was discounted,
as it fails to contribute towards the Council’s Net Zero
targets or capture the external investment offered by the APC.
topline: The Service Director for Operations & Environmental Services has decided to repower a Council-owned Refuse Collection Vehicle with an electric driveline using grant funding.

Assistant Director for Place and Economy, copies of which had been

The committee had previously approved a
strategy for the replacement of the Council’s HGV fleet and
agreed principles for the replacement of the smaller fleet. It
agreed to formally review the strategy in 2027.
 
The Committee gave delegated authority to the
Director for Sustainability and Resources, in consultation with the
Adur Cabinet Member for Finance and Resources and the Worthing
Member for Resources, to proceed with the implementation of the
fleet replacement program, including initiating and concluding
procurement processes and entering into contracts for the supply of
containers and vehicles for the service.
 
In the financial year 2025/26 the HGV fleet
was being replaced in line with the strategy. The smaller fleet was
also being replaced within the parameters agreed by JSC in February
2025.
 
Members were asked to revise the proposals for
the 2026/27 HGV replacement program in light of cost pressures, the
need to properly test electric RCV technology and in recognition of
the fact that the fleet now ran on Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO)
rather than diesel which is had resulted in significantly reduced
carbon emissions. 
 
 
Decision:
 

1.    
That the progress on the implementation of the Fleet Replacement
Strategy adopted in February 2025 be noted, which includes
transitioning the entire fleet to Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil (HVO)
and the procurement of nine new refuse collection vehicles (RCVs) -
one electric and eight with internal combustion engines (ICE).
 

2.    
That it be noted that officers are working on a grant funded
project to convert an existing ICE RCV in the fleet to an electric
drive train. As part of the project the vehicle body will be
refurbished. The project is currently going through the final
stages of internal governance before sign off. 
 

3.    
That the the following changes to the
Fleet Replacement Strategy 2026/27 be agreed:
 
a.    
Delay a further decision on the procurement of e-RCVs until
February 2027 to allow the service to test the e-RCV which is on
order, and potentially, subject to project sign off, test the e-RCV
converted vehicle mentioned above.
 
b.    
Approve the purchase of eight new ICE RCVs and the refurbishment of
three of the existing RCV fleet to ensure service resilience and
continue to flatten the vehicle replacement curve as agreed in
February 2025.
 
c.    
Approve the commissioning of a detailed cost and feasibility study
to inform the options to upgrade the infrastructure at Commerce Way
depot to accommodate a large scale electric fleet.
 
 

4.    
That a further report being brought to this committee in early 2027
to confirm the fleet replacement program for 2027/28 informed by
the experience of running at least one e-RCV and the findings of
the feasibility study mentioned in 2.3.3 above.

Project as approved by the Joint Strategic Committee on the 8th
July 2025

The £400,000.00 funding is the Borough
Councils match funding contribution to the Environment Agency led
coastal defence capital maintenance project (circa
£5,000,000.00) undertaking repairs to existing timber groynes
to extend their life span for a further ten years as part of a

Before the Committee was a report by the
Director for Housing and Communities, copies of which had been
circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to the
signed copy of these minutes as item 7.
 
This report before members set out the
proposed new Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy, 2025-2030,
which is due for renewal and is central to the Councils’
ambitions set out in the Corporate Plan - Fair, Green and Local.
Having a home was a fundamental need and right for local residents. The strategy provided an important
strategic and statutory framework, which set out the strategic
aspiration of the councils’- working with partner
organisations - to prevent and manage homelessness, and when it
occurs, and - as set out in the strategy - for it to be brief and
non-recurring.
 
The strategy was required to meet the
Councils’ legal duties in relation to homelessness. It served
as a key delivery framework as part of the recently adopted Adur
and Worthing Housing Strategy 2025-2030, aligning fully with its
overarching principles and supporting Priority 4: "Preventing
homelessness and rough sleeping”
 
This was a key document for the Councils,
especially given the immense funding pressures relating to
homelessness, which are especially acute for Worthing Council.
These demand pressures could not be solely managed by our teams.
This work needed a systems approach focusing on prevention and
early intervention.
 
The strategic approach had been prepared
during a time of immense change including the Ministry of Housing,
Communities and Local Governments (MHCLG) new strategy, ‘A
National Plan to End Homelessness’ (Appendix 1), new national
legislative changes, including the Renters Rights Act, the
Supported Housing Regulatory Oversight Act and Local Government
Reorganisation. The development of the Delivery Plan would be
co-produced and supported through the Adur and Worthing
Homelessness Prevention Partnership.
 
 
Decision:
 

1)   
That the new strategy for Adur and Worthing Councils 2025 - 2030 be
noted and approved as set out in Appendix 2.
 

2)   
That it be noted that the initial priorities set out within this
strategic document will be used to form a Delivery Plan. This will
be co-produced with the Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Prevention
Partnership covering the first 18 months of this strategy.
 

3)   
That the Committee receive a report on the delivery of the strategy
to this committee on an annual basis.
 

4)   
That it be noted that the strategy had been produced during a time
of immense change including the new National Plan to End
Homelessness (just published), new national legislative changes,
including the Renters Rights Act and the Supported Housing
Regulatory Oversight Act and Local Government Reorganisation.
 

5)   
That authority be delegated to the Director for Communities and
Housing, in consultation with each Councils’ cabinet
portfolio leads for Housing and Citizen’s Services, to make
amendments to the strategies Delivery Plan, in response to the
development of these wider strategic changes and service demands
and as priorities are co-produced with the Adur and Worthing
Homelessness Prevention Partnership.
 
Call In: The call-in deadline for
decisions will be 5.00pm on 16 January 2026.
topline: The Joint Strategic Committee has decided to approve the new Homelessness and Rough Sleeping Strategy for Adur and Worthing Councils, aiming to prevent and manage homelessness in the area.

Before the Committee was a report by the
Assistant Director for Place and Economy, copies of which had been
circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to the
signed copy of these minutes as item 8.
 
The purpose of the report before Members was
to update Members on the recent work undertaken to identify a path
to secure a long term future for the
Lido, including further specialist surveyor reports commissioned in
the last 1 - 3 years.
 
The report represented a pragmatic strategy to
progress with the safeguarding of the asset by the Council
prioritising effort to assemble the necessary funding to safeguard
the structural integrity of the asset. And, within that strategy,
recognise that due to the complex nature of the asset and the
current economic climate, that this would need a dedicated effort
over the next couple of years.
 
The current critical structural state of the
lido was acknowledged, as well as its significant heritage value
and the importance of formulating this plan now to prevent further
decline and preserve its future, especially now ahead of Local
Government Reorganisation (LGR).
 
The strategy would involve working with the
community, businesses and key stakeholders, including West Sussex
County Council via the Growth Deal, to assemble the funding to
support the delivery of repairing the substructure and enable a
sympathetic and robust process to secure a long
term investment partner.
 
 
Decision:
 

1)   
That the renewed approach to bring forward the Lido to secure its
future and endorse the phased plan in sections 5, 6, 7 and 8 be
noted.
 

2)   
That it be noted that, at the request of Historic England, that
further structural testing to be undertaken in early 2026 to help
inform a solution for the substructure, utilising remaining funding
in the capital programme of up to £70k (remaining Lido
budget).
 

3)   
That a progress report be brought back to JSC later in 26/27,
specifically in reference to phase 1.
 
Call In: The call-in deadline for
decisions will be 5.00pm on 16 January 2026.
topline: The Joint Strategic Committee has decided to move forward with plans to secure the future of a historic Lido by assembling necessary funding and conducting further structural testing.

To award the wayfinding contract, which
includes design and manufacture, to Tara Signs Ltd, following a
procurement exercise, in the sum of £35,974. The project,
funded by the UK Shared Prosperity Fund and Pooled Business Rates,
will install eight new monoliths across the town centre, similar in
design to the installation in Railway Approach, to assist residents
and visitors accessing different parts of the town centre and
seafront through new wayfinding infrastructure. This decision
includes the manufacture and map elements, Items from the quotation
received.

The Council has been engaging with businesses
in the town centre and the need for improved and more visible
wayfinding is the top priority. The age, condition and design of
existing wayfinding in the town centre is in need of upgrading and
this project is critical to ensure residents and visitors can
‘wayfind’ throughout the town centre and seafront. In
addition, this is being funded by UK Shared Prosperity Funding
(UKSPF) with a deadline of 31st March 2026 for these funds to be
spent. A decision is required now to meet the implementation /
installation timelines.

These are as follows:
 

1.   
Reduce number of monoliths - this may compromise the impact of the
scheme by omitting areas and gateways, which would go against
feedback received from businesses.

2.   
Have digital monoliths managed by a third party- this would
represent additional challenges from install to sustainability as
well as the impact on the look and feel of the town centre as it
would involve external advertising amongst the wayfinding.
topline: The Assistant Director Place & Economy has decided to award a contract to Tara Signs Ltd for the design and manufacture of new wayfinding infrastructure in the town center.

Following a price review from the two highest
scoring Contractors, and confirmation that both Contractors will
stand by their tendered prices, following the competitive Tender
process completed late 2024, the decision is to award the Phase 2
Replacement Fire Damper Works to Gemini AMPM Ltd in the sum of
£106,749.00 plus VAT and Fees. The works will replace the
existing defective Fire Dampers so as to ensure the fire safety of
the building remains compliant.

Fire dampers are a key part of a building's
life safety features; they close in the event of a fire and prevent
smoke spread through the ventilation system. The fire dampers at
the Splashpoint Leisure Centre have
suffered corrosion and are in various states of disrepair.
Replacement and repair of the fire dampers is required to maintain
a safe environment for users and staff. A specialist Consulting
Engineer has been appointed to prepare a prioritised programme of
works; this is the second Phase of repairs.

There are no alternative options for this type
of work in order to keep the Leisure Centre Compliant from a Fire
Safety Perspective.
topline: The Assistant Director Place & Economy has decided to award the Phase 2 Replacement Fire Damper Works to Gemini AMPM Ltd to ensure fire safety compliance at Splashpoint Leisure Centre.

Before the Committee was a report by the Chief

copy of which is attached to the signed copy of these minutes as
Item 6.
 
The report before members presents the final
version of the new corporate strategy for Adur & Worthing
Councils for the period 2025-2028, entitled 'Fair, Green &
Local', including the Delivery Plan and Equality Impact Assessment.
Following the endorsement of the direction of travel by the Joint
Strategic Committee in October 2025, a period of further engagement
with staff, community leaders, and the Joint Overview &
Scrutiny Committee has been undertaken. The strategy presented
incorporated the feedback and established the framework for the
Councils’ work over three years, whilst acknowledging that
significant additional work programmes relating to Local Government
Reform were likely to impact on the councils’ capacity and
required the delivery plan to be continually reviewed.
 
'Fair, Green & Local' represented an
evolution of the previous "Our Plan," adapted to meet the
challenges of ongoing financial pressures and the transition toward
Local Government Reform (LGR). It formalised the shift to an
"enabler and catalyst" operating model, prioritising partnership
working to deliver outcomes that the Councils could not achieve
alone.
 
The Chief Executive introduced the report to
the Committee and notified the Committee of some amendments. The
plan was being adapted so that the councils could work with partner
agencies such as the National Park and the wildlife trust to plan a
multi partner engagement with the community at a thriving together
meeting in March. On a point of clarification and change, a status
in a previous report was ‘awaiting funding’ in the
delivery plan. This had been amended to ‘in
development’ as awaiting funding was an active process of
finding funds
 
Decision:
 

1.    
That the Committee formally endorses the 'Fair, Green & Local'
Corporate Strategy (2025-2028) and the associated Delivery Plan
attached as Appendix 1 to the report
 

2.    
That the findings of the Equality Impact Assessment (attached as
Appendix 2) and the mitigations set out therein be noted.
 

3.    
That authority be delegated  to the
Chief Executive, in consultation with the Leaders, to make
amendments to the Strategy and Delivery Plan as required, such
amendments to be reported to the Joint Strategic Committee as part
of regular quarterly performance updates (with the first being
March 2026).
 

4.    
That it be recommended to Adur District Council and Worthing
Borough Council the adoption of Councils 'Fair, Green & Local'
Corporate Strategy (2025-2028) and the associated Delivery Plan
attached as Appendix 1.

Before the Committee was a report by the
Interim Director for Core Services, copies of which had been
circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to the
signed copy of these minutes as item 7.
 
This report presented an update on the budget
setting process for 2026/27 for both councils as well as updating
on the progress of the implementation of the financial strategy.
Progress on the financial strategy was being impacted in the short
term from budget pressures caused by external factors particularly
housing demand.
 
The Local Government Finance Policy Statement
announced final decisions on the Fair Funding 2.0 reforms and
published a finance policy statement setting out the key parameters
for local government funding from 2026-27 to 2028-29. Ministers had
confirmed they will go ahead with most of the changes proposed in
the original consultation, in particular:
 
? Major changes to the main funding formula
with a stronger link to levels of deprivation and population
?  Resetting the
baseline for retained business rates in full in 2026-27
?  Abolishing the
New Homes Bonus
? Simplifying and consolidating several grant
pots, including grants for homelessness prevention and rough
sleeping
 
Ministers have made several significant
changes to the original proposals:
 
? Updating the Index of Multiple Deprivation
data and methodology in the main funding formula to reflect housing
costs more strongly.
? Removing the remoteness uplift from the main
funding formula, except for adult social care costs.
?  Reducing the
weighting in the funding formula for visitor and commuter
population.
? Preserving Recovery Grant allocations at
2025-26 levels for the whole of the spending review period.
? Introducing a more generous funding floor
for councils that have responsibility for social care and currently
receive the Recovery Grant.
 
MHCLG had confirmed that the council tax
referendum threshold will remain at 3% or £5 (whichever is
greater) for district councils. Social care authorities will
continue to be able to raise an additional 2% precept.
 
The Government will provide new burdens
funding for the ongoing revenue cost of operating weekly food waste
collections . However, the funding will be rolled into the finance
settlement and distributed via the main funding formula rather than
via a specific grant. This meant there would be no transparency
about how much burden funding was provided and a likelihood that
some, if not all, councils would be underfunded for the costs of
introducing a full food waste collection service.
 
Whilst some assumptions had been made on the
potential funding that may come from the new fairer funding
process, there was a significant level of uncertainty on the local
impact of the new assessment formula. The allocation across
individual councils would not be visible until the provisional
settlement which was not expected until the week commencing 15th
December.
 
Despite the considerable work being done to
implement a more resilient and sustainable financial strategy, it
was clear that it is unlikely to provide the funding required to
close the significant budget gap in Worthing and so the proposed
route for requesting exceptional funding support (EFS) which is
outlined in the policy statement is necessary. Members are being
recommended to request the chief executive formally write to the
Ministry for Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) to
request this continued support for Worthing for 2026/27.
 
 
 
Decision:
 

1.    
That the contents of the report including the working 5-year
forecasts as at appendix 1 be noted.
 

2.    
That the chief executive be requested to write to MHCLG in order to
request exceptional financial support for Worthing in order to get
the help needed to balance the 2026/27 revenue budget and
additional support for 2025/26.
 
 
Call In: The call-in deadline for
decisions will be 5.00pm on 19 December 2025

content:
The Worthing Heat Network project is
delivering low carbon heating to council and other buildings, with
an implementation date of October 2025. 
This will include Worthing Theatre buildings: Assembly Hall,
Connaught Theatre, Pavilion Theatre and Museum.  The project will deliver key benefits, including
£4.3m of grant and council funded enabling works in the
buildings, including replacement windows, lighting, glazing and
mechanical & electrical improvements, along with the key
benefit of removing gas boilers and transitioning to low carbon
heat (hot water) from renewable sources.
 
Whilst national policy is expected over the
next few years to reduce the price of electricity and increase the
price of gas as part of the national net zero 2050 strategy, at
present low carbon heating is more expensive than gas.  The Worthing Heat Network scheme is guaranteed
through various controls to provide the lowest cost low carbon
heating option, but does not currently compete with gas fossil
fuel.
 
Forward thinking organisations such the
Worthing Council, Worthing Hospital, Worthing Theatres and South
Downs Leisure are making the transition now.
 
As part of signing supply agreements relating
to DforS&R/027/23-24, Worthing Theatres are expected to
experience a significant increase to their annual energy bill and
require transitional support as budgets are
re-adjusted.  This is a result of the
central government grant funding formula and the split between
capital and revenue costs in the financial model.  This level of increase is not being experienced by
other buildings and organisations in the network.
 
Worthing Theatres are strong supporters of the
Heat Network, and the Council has been in discussions with WTM on a
range of issues, including the transitional financial issue which
has been under negotiation.
 
As part of the contract with Worthing Heat
Network Limited (ESCO), a payment of £60k is being made to
the Council for a period of 5 years, starting in
2024/25.  This budget is unallocated,
although it will be required for heat network zone coordination
support from 2027/28, in liaison with the new Sussex strategic
authority which will have (funded) responsibility for zone
coordination once it is established.
 
It has therefore been possible to propose that
some of these funds be used to mitigate the impact of the revenue
costs of connecting to the heat network for Worthing
Theatres.  Agreement has been reached
that a total of £110k will be provided to WTM by the Council
over a two year period (2025-2027) to smooth the transition and
allow WTM to adjust budgets to the higher cost of low carbon
heating.

To enable Worthing Theatres to be able to
enter into a direct supply agreement with Worthing Heat Network
Limited (ESCO) and therefore to ensure grant monies for enabling
works can be drawn down from central government before the
deadline.

Negotiations have been on-going for some time
with the financial issue as a key barrier to progress.  This solution does not put pressure on core
council budgets, but alleviates the considerable financial shock of
increased bills to WTM.
topline: The Chief Executive has decided to provide financial support to Worthing Theatres to ease the transition to low carbon heating through the Worthing Heat Network project.

Council Tax Support was a scheme to help some
people pay their Council Tax. This depended on their income and
personal circumstances and was only available to some people in the
UK who are living on a low income.
 
The Council Tax Support scheme must be
considered each year as part of the Local Government Finance Act
2012 (which introduced the framework for localism of Council Tax
Support), with members confirming revisions, continuing the scheme
as is or replacing with another scheme.
 
This Scheme formed an important part of the
councils’ ambition for Fair, Green and Local by supporting
people who are living on the lowest incomes. Whilst the councils
were both experiencing budgetary pressures, the scheme was one way
in which the councils were responding to the enduring impacts of
poverty. The councils’ Proactive programme had been one
response to this, focusing early help and support for residents
experiencing vulnerabilities.
 
Given the importance of the scheme, the report
asked members of both councils to continue the scheme with no
changes and to recommend this to the Full Councils in respect of
2026/27.
 
Decision:
 

1.   
That the report be noted
 

2.   
That it be recommended to Adur District Council that the Council
Tax Support scheme in respect of working age customers for 2026/27
should:
 
a.   
Be based upon the current Council Tax Support scheme for 2025/26
with no restrictions; and

 
b.   
Not be further altered with any other changes beyond necessary
technical amendments required to keep the scheme consistent with
the national rules in respect of Housing Benefit

content:
That the award of £30,060 to Apron
Creative CIC for development of the Apron Community Farm project on
Adur Council land at Old Salts Farm is approved.
 

Adur District Council owns land at Old Salts
Farm, Lancing which was previously home to Riverside Equestrian
Centre, tenants who surrendered their lease in 2024.  The
council subsequently issued an expression of interest which
attracted 7 applications, some of which were commercial operators
or businesses, and not deemed appropriate for the site.  2
community/social value based applications were taken through to
full business plan development.  One application was a
proposal to support the homeless through practical learning with
car repair, and the other was Apron Community Farm which included
regenerative farming features such as a polytunnel, herb garden and
orchard, as well as sites for wellbeing and therapy sessions, an
educational space, an area for a children’s forest school,
ponds and workshop spaces for traditional craftspeople to share
their skills.  This application was assessed by a panel of
officers as most suitable for the location, delivering a range of
benefits and outcomes, particularly local community
involvement.

The council is keen to see the site regenerated for the benefit of
the local community and recognises the costs involved in developing
the project to the stage that further external funding can be
secured.  Following consideration at the Joint Strategic
Committee, October 2025 as part of the councils wider Fair, Green
and Local strategy, as well as Nature Vision, the Adur Cabinet
Member for Environment & Leisure is asked to consider the
release of £30,060 to support Phase 1 Project
Development.  Apron Creative CIC have launched a Crowdfunder
in parallel to this request, is securing a range of pro bono
support, and has also submitted a funding proposal to the National
Heritage Lottery Fund for £55,000 for the project’s
Phase 3.

In making this decision for Phase 1 funding, it should be
recognised that delivery of the final project will be reliant on
the securing of future phases of funding, including Phase 2, which
is not yet secured.

A considerable amount of unpaid volunteering
time has already been committed to the project.  Apron
Community Farm promises to transform an unused piece of public land
into a vibrant community facility, with additional natural flood
management benefits through the proposed wetland scheme.
 
Given the EOI process did not generate any
suitable alternatives, if the project does not receive development
funding, it is likely that the land will remain unused, with the
additional risk that the Local Government Reform process underway
will further reduce the likelihood of active project work at this
site for some years to come.
topline: The Chief Executive has decided to award £30,060 to Apron Creative CIC for the development of the Apron Community Farm project on Adur Council land at Old Salts Farm.

To dispose of land for a term of 99 years in
conjunction with the installation of the Worthing Heat Network
project. This is part of the ongoing project which commenced in
2022.
 

Pipeline leases for the Worthing Heat Network
would be granted.
 
Homefield Park:
To allow for the installation of a necessary
section of the network’s underground pipework.  Granting
a 99 year lease of the subsoil allows for the long term
installation of the pipes which are essential for supporting low
carbon heat to connect buildings and achieve the network’s
goal of decarbonizing the town’s energy supply. This is a key
step in the project to reduce carbon emissions and provide cheaper
heating options for the community.
 
Lease purpose:  A lease of the
subsoil is the legal mechanism for the council to allow Hemiko, the
project’s developer, to install and maintain this pipework
beneath the park with a 99 year lease being appropriate for this
purpose. 
 
High Street Energy
Centre:
To allow for the installation of a necessary
part of electrical infrastructure to connect the Energy Centre (EC)
to the National Electricity Grid.  Granting a 99 year lease of
the subsoil allows for the installation of a substation which is
essential to supporting low carbon heat from the EC and achieve the
network’s goal of decarbonizing the town’s energy
supply. This is a key step in the project to reduce carbon
emissions and provide cheaper heating options for the
community.
 
Lease purpose:  Allowing the
energy provider to utilise the land space on a 99 year lease and
set up and provide electricity to the Hemiko Energy Centre to allow
them to run the Low Carbon Air Source Heat Pumps
(ASHPs) 
 
Community benefits (that applies to both
sites as a whole) Once completed the network aims to provide
cheaper  low carbon heating to residents and businesses with
the pipeline installation in both locations being a crucial step in
making this possible.
 
Project necessity (that applies to both
sites as a whole) The Worthing Heat Network requires a network
of underground pipes to distribute heat from its energy centre to
connected buildings like the Town  Hall, the hospital and the
Pavilion Theatre.
 

None.
topline: The Interim Chief Executive has decided to grant 99-year leases for the installation of essential infrastructure in Worthing as part of the ongoing Heat Network project.

Before the Committee was a report by the
Interim Director for Core Services, copies of which had been
circulated to all Members and a copy of which is attached to the
signed copy of these minutes as Item 9.
 
The Vision for nature provided a strategic
framework for the long-term recovery of nature across Adur and
Worthing. It was designed to guide the work of the Councils and
their partners, and act as a catalyst for community and business
engagement in enhancing the natural environment.
 
The purpose of the report before members was
to seek the Committee's approval to adopt the Vision as a guiding
document. This would enable the Councils to align their resources
and efforts, and to proactively seek external funding and
partnerships to deliver the ambitions outlined within the paper.
Endorsement would position Adur and Worthing as leaders in local
nature recovery, contributing effectively to regional and national
environmental targets.
 
The report also sought support to progress
with a number of related key initiatives
across Adur and Worthing; these include the Cissbury Fields project, a new Pesticides Policy, a
review of urban street tree planting and works supporting Adur
River restoration.
 
Decision:
 

1.   
That 'A Vision for Nature in Adur & Worthing' be endorsed as an
enabling framework to guide the Councils' actions in further
protecting and enhancing biodiversity, building external
partnerships and empowering community action.
 

2.   
That the Pesticides Policy be formally adopted to reinforce the
Councils’ commitment to supporting the environment through
safe and good practice.
 

3.   
That the Trees for Streets programme 2022-2025 be reviewed and an
urban street tree planting and maintenance strategy be developed
across Adur & Worthing for presentation and decision
at November Joint Strategic
Committee.
 

4.   
That the ongoing support and work in partnership with Friends of
the Adur SSSI (Site of Special Scientific Interest) and Apron
towards Adur River restoration and renaturing be noted.
 

5.   
That the principle of project funding from Shoreham Harbour Growth
Funds be supported subject to decision by the Cabinet Member for
Environment & Leisure (Adur) for the provision of wayfinding
signage and introduction of educational materials for Adur SSSI and
Apron.

decisions will be 5.00pm on 21 October 2025

In July 2025 the councils approved their

enabling more coordinated and realistic programmes of activity

statutory obligations of the councils
 
The Medium Term

developed with the strategic reviews informing that work, together
with other economic factors.
 
Work continued to ensure a balanced budget
while acknowledging the ongoing uncertainties around future funding
arrangements. The report before members presented the next step in

represented a snapshot of the budget development in order to provide greater transparency. The work
plan for the implementation of the new financial strategy ensured
that the different elements of the new strategy would be live and
active in order to support the setting
of the 26/27 budget and help the organisation look beyond that
point with more certainty. While the financial situation continued
to be challenging the budget reflected the considerable work going
